articles.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ - The Guardian
articles.summary: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.
Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.
The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.
Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.
Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.
Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.
- Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claim - The Guardian
articles.summary: Ukraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claim  The GuardianTrump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'  BBCPutin has already broken Trump's 'energy ceasefire' with attack on power plant, says Zelenskyy  Sky NewsTrump claims Ukraine and Russia have agreed to energy ceasefire | CNN Politics  CNNTrump’s fantasy ceasefire tricks no one  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
- Russian strikes hit multiple Ukrainian power plants after Donald Trump claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The Ukrainian president said on social media a drone had hit a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday, leading to power outages in the capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on the CHP-5 power plant in the eastern city of Kharkiv, adding:“Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ [drones] all day.”
- Trump said earlier that “effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” the US president wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning in Washington, without further details. Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me” and he was seeking further details. Russia has yet to confirm it agreed.
- The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine’s key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission. British prime minister Andy Burnham said a sustained energy ceasefire was “the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets”. French president Emmanuel Macron said Paris supported a “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine.
- Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed six people in two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, including a strike on a grocery store in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, where three people died and 20 were injured. Two children were among the injured, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In a separate attack in western Ukraine, officials said a Russian strike killed three people.
- Trump’s energy truce claim came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel while temporarily easing US sanctions, prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney added to the chorus of disapproval after a Sunday call with Zelenskyy, saying the diesel deal “is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe”. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed Zelenskyy “as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom”, while Germany foreign minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin continued to “fully support” him.
- Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy when asked about criticism of the Russia diesel deal, saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” who would finally settle the war. Zelenskyy pushed back, telling US ABC News on Sunday: “First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader.”
- The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times quoted officials in Europe as saying. The US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries, they said.
- A Ukrainian drone killed one person in Russia’s border Belgorod region on Sunday, officials said. The operational headquarters in Belgorod region said the drone struck a car on a road near the border. In the part of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region held by Russian forces, Moscow-installed officials said one person had been killed in a Ukrainian attack.
- Russia’s military said it struck a logistics centre in southern Ukraine’s Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea. The logistics centre in the town of Ternivka was used to store military and dual-use cargoes for the Ukrainian military, the Russian defence ministry claimed on Sunday.

articles.title: NATO Is Winning the War Russia Isn’t Fighting - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: NATO Is Winning the War Russia Isn’t Fighting  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
On 23 September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter flying from Kaliningrad crossed into Polish airspace north of the town of Braniewo, penetrated roughly 300 metres and stayed for 42 seconds before turning back. Polish fighter jets were scrambled, ground-based air defences went on standby, and Poland’s Operational Command concluded that Russia was once again testing the readiness of its air defences. By any measurable standard, it was a non-event. No shots were fired, nothing was damaged and nobody was hurt. That is exactly why it matters.
Twelve days later, the head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service told the Bundestag that Russia is waging a “shadow war” against Germany. Within days, the Atlantic Council published a report arguing that years of reinforcing NATO’s eastern flank have done little to discourage Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. The convergence is notable. European intelligence services, the EU’s defence commissioner and a leading Washington think tank are now describing the same problem in almost identical terms. NATO has become very good at deterring a war Russia is not currently trying to fight, and remains poorly equipped for the one it is fighting.
A conflict without a threshold
Hybrid warfare is not a new concept, and neither is the vocabulary used to describe it. What has changed is its texture. A US Helsinki Commission study grouped Russian operations inside NATO territory into four categories: attacks on critical infrastructure, violence campaigns, weaponised migration, and election interference and information operations. The Atlantic Council’s Agnia Grigas adds a more troubling observation: these operations increasingly carry a kinetic component and are persistent rather than episodic, forming a continuous pressure campaign rather than a series of isolated provocations.
Poland’s recent months illustrate the pattern. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile entered Polish airspace and came down in a field in the east of the country. On 15 September, an unidentified drone approached the US ballistic missile defence base at Redzikowo. Two days later, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned of a real risk that drones or missiles could fly into eastern-flank states and cause destruction. Then came the helicopter, which appears to be the first publicly reported case of a Russian military helicopter crossing Poland’s land border. In Germany, the intelligence chief Martin Jäger pointed to an attempted Russian drone attack on Leipzig airport on 31 July.
None of these incidents, taken individually, comes close to triggering Article 5. That is the design. Each is calibrated to sit beneath the threshold at which collective defence is invoked, while remaining visible enough to probe defences, signal intent and impose costs: scrambled jets, closed airspace, diverted resources and political anxiety. The cumulative effect is to normalise a higher baseline of risk. What would have been a crisis in 2021 is a routine Wednesday in 2026.
Moscow rejects this characterisation entirely. Its embassy has insisted that Russia poses no threat to NATO and has no intention of confronting it. Attribution in individual cases is sometimes contested, and analysts should resist folding every incident into a single narrative. But German, Danish and Polish authorities have assessed the pattern independently, and their conclusions are consistent enough that the burden of explanation has shifted.
Built for the wrong war
NATO’s conventional posture has been transformed since 2022. Defence budgets have risen, eastern-flank battlegroups have expanded, and Poland is building a network of bunkers, barriers, sensors and potential minefields along its borders with Belarus and Kaliningrad, with similar work under way in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. The Atlantic Council estimates that Russia maintains around 40,000 ground troops in the wider Baltic region, a figure it believes could be raised to roughly 100,000 by shifting forces from western Russia.
That investment is not wasted. A credible conventional defence is the reason a large-scale invasion remains unlikely, and Jäger himself said the BND sees no signs that Russia is preparing one. But this is where the asymmetry lies. Deterring conventional formations is now well resourced; countering persistent grey-zone pressure remains fragmented. The alliance’s decision-making is built around a binary, attack or no attack, with Article 5 as the hinge. Russia’s strategy is to operate permanently in the space between.
There is an uncomfortable irony here. The more credible NATO’s conventional deterrence becomes, the more rational it is for Moscow to shift pressure downward, into the domain where acting is cheapest and punishment is hardest. Success on one rung of the escalation ladder pushes the contest onto another.
The case for making Moscow pay, and why it is harder than it sounds
Grigas’s prescription is straightforward. Allies must persuade the Kremlin that hostile action carries predictable, material costs, using a pre-agreed menu of options: targeted sanctions, restrictions on Russian and Belarusian travel, trade and transit, large-scale diplomatic expulsions and cyber operations. Future drone incursions, attempted assassinations and sabotage, she argues, should prompt responses that are proportionate, coordinated and pre-agreed rather than mere condemnation. The EU’s defence commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, has said answers to hybrid attacks should be as painful as the attacks themselves. Kurt Volker, a former US ambassador to NATO, has asked openly where the line is that Russia would have to cross to provoke a response.
The argument has obvious appeal. Predictability is the core of deterrence, and Russia arguably exploits ambiguity in NATO’s responses more than ambiguity in its own actions. Yet the proposal runs into three problems that its advocates tend to understate.
The first is attribution. Hybrid operations are built for deniability, and Jäger has warned that Moscow may use false-flag operations designed to conceal the real perpetrator and complicate the response. An automatic response requires an agreed standard of proof, and 32 governments with different intelligence capacities and risk tolerances will not easily converge on one. A mechanism that fires on contested attribution hands Moscow a propaganda victory. One that waits for certainty is not automatic.
The second is consensus. The costs of retaliation fall unevenly. Restricting transit to Kaliningrad is borne disproportionately by Lithuania; measures against Belarus land hardest on Poland and Latvia. A menu agreed in Brussels must be executed in capitals with very different exposures, and some governments in both NATO and the EU have repeatedly shown reluctance to sign up to new measures against Russia.
The third is escalation. Part of the logic of the grey zone is that it allows both sides to avoid a war neither wants. A published schedule of penalties raises the cost of provocation, but it also hands initiative to whoever defines the triggers, and gives Moscow a map of exactly where to operate just beneath them. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte’s insistence that the alliance has response options that are not always public and not always tit for tat is often read as complacency. It can equally be read as a judgement that strategic ambiguity is itself a deterrent. That position deserves more serious engagement than its critics usually give it.
Germany moves to the front line
The most significant shift in this week’s debate is geographic. For years, “front line” in European security discourse meant the Baltic states, Poland and Romania. Jäger’s testimony relocated it. He said that no other country poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany than Russia, which he argued is imposing the confrontation on Berlin because of its support for Ukraine and the Baltic states. He also warned that it would be a great illusion to assume the conflict with Russia will end when the war in Ukraine does.
That last point is the analytical core of the issue. If the shadow war is not a by-product of the war in Ukraine but a durable feature of Russian–European relations, then treating it as a crisis to be managed until a ceasefire is a category error. It becomes a permanent condition to be governed, through infrastructure resilience, investigative and prosecutorial capacity, intelligence sharing and the political willingness to name perpetrators publicly. European authorities are growing bolder in publicly identifying the states and organisations they hold responsible, which is a necessary first step.
It also raises an institutional question that the debate tends to skip: who owns this problem? Much of what Russia targets, including airports, rail networks, energy grids, undersea cables and elections, falls within national law enforcement and EU competences rather than NATO’s military remit. The alliance can deter armoured divisions; it cannot investigate a sabotage cell in Leipzig. The EU holds the regulatory, sanctions and legal tools, while NATO holds the military signalling. The deterrence gap persists partly because neither institution fully owns it.
What closing the gap would actually require
A credible response is less likely to come from a single new doctrine than from tightening the seams between existing ones. That means a shared attribution framework that allows faster, coordinated public attribution; sanctions packages drafted in advance and held in reserve, so that speed does not depend on fresh negotiation among 27 or 32 governments; infrastructure resilience treated as a core component of defence spending rather than an afterthought; and a clearer division of labour between NATO and the EU on hybrid threats.

articles.title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns - BBC
articles.summary: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns  BBC'Tax rises needed to plug £35bn gap' and 'Putin breaks Trump's 'ceasefire"  BBCUK's Healey can't risk a 'steady as you go' budget, think tank warns  ReutersIFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK spending pressures  The GuardianHealey Needs £35 Billion to Meet UK Spending Plans, IFS Says  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.
Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.
It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up.
The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation".
However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.
"But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together."
He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".
However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.
The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring.
"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said.
"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.
"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.
The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.
These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps.
The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.
Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.
'Breathing space'
Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30.
However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues.
But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).
Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale.
However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion.
The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra £25bn in 2029-30.
That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises.
The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different.
But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time.
It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans.
However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line.

articles.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?  Al JazeeraEthiopia says it must defend itself against Eritrea's 'all-out invasion'  ReutersEthiopia and Eritrea are on the brink of another conflict  The EconomistEthiopia tells UN it is acting in self-defense against Eritrea  AP NewsEthiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops enter Tigray  BBC
articles.full_text:
Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.
The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces.
Recommended Stories
The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war.
However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea.
So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war?
What did Eritrea and Ethiopia say at the UN?
Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty.
In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.
He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking.
Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”.
He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.
The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”.
“The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera.
Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.
Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts.
“Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera.
He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said.
“The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.”
What is the latest fighting about, and how is Eritrea allegedly involved?
Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city.
In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force.
Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi.
It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting.
Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims.
The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development.
Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified.
The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement.
That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger.
The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorated.
Has Ethiopia sent troops north towards Eritrea?
Multiple media reports say Ethiopian government troops and allied militias entered Adigrat, a strategic city roughly 30km (19 miles) from the Eritrean border, on Saturday.
Three residents confirmed their presence to Reuters, while verified footage showed government-allied militia members walking through the city.
Associated Press news agency footage also showed Ethiopian military vehicles entering Adigrat as some residents welcomed the troops.
Government-allied forces have reported capturing Idaga Hamus and Abiy-Adi, while explosions and alleged drone strikes have been reported near Adigrat.
Are Ethiopia and Eritrea inching towards war?
Analysts warn that Ethiopia and Eritrea may already have moved beyond threats and into a dangerous phase of possible military confrontation.
BISI’s Ibrahim said the two countries have moved beyond “inching” towards war, noting that “The situation has entered a high-risk phase of limited but direct military confrontation with a real possibility of rapid escalation into interstate war.”
He warned that the severing of diplomatic ties removed the “last formal mechanism for crisis management”, while Ethiopian military advances towards the Eritrean border increased the risk of “miscalculation”.
Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist, said the current tensions should be understood in the context of decades of hostility between the neighbours.
Their brief alliance during the 2020-2022 Tigray war was an exception and was driven by a shared hostility towards the TPLF, Gardner told Al Jazeera.
“The Ethiopian government’s strategic goal number one is access to the Red Sea, but also removing Eritrea’s government from the picture,” he noted.
“It’s very much looking like the most dangerous moment for the region since that 1998 to 2000 war.”
Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said.
“The central danger is not necessarily that either government has decided to launch a full-scale war, but that military miscalculations, mutual distrust and domestic political pressures could trigger a further escalation neither side can easily control.
“A wider conflict is not inevitable, but the space for diplomatic de-escalation is rapidly narrowing,” he said.

articles.title: The ICC faces scrutiny and political pushback as it investigates global war crimes and pursues high-profile suspects. - Awani International
articles.summary: The ICC faces scrutiny and political pushback as it investigates global war crimes and pursues high-profile suspects.  Awani International
articles.full_text:
AI Brief
- The International Criminal Court, established in 2002, prosecutes war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and aggression, with 125 member states and a 196 million euro budget for 2026.
- The ICC has issued 68 arrest warrants, including for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and is investigating cases in Palestine, Ukraine, Africa, Venezuela, Myanmar, and the Philippines.
- The United States opposes ICC jurisdiction over its nationals, imposing sanctions on ICC officials after warrants for US allies, and has never joined the court.
THE HAGUE, NETHERLANDS: South African judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, who was awarded the Nobel peace prize on Friday (October 9), has been a judge on several international courts, including the International Criminal Court. Here are some facts about this court:
WHEN WAS THE ICC SET UP AND WHY?
The court was established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression when member states are unwilling or unable to do so themselves. It can prosecute crimes committed by nationals of member states or on the territory of member states by other actors. It has 125 member states. The court's budget for 2026 is about €196 million euros (US$2220 million)
WHAT IS THE ICC INVESTIGATING?
The ICC is conducting investigations in the Palestinian territories, Ukraine, African states such as Sudan, Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, Venezuela, Myanmar and the Philippines. It says there have been 34 cases before the court, some with more than one defendant. ICC judges have issued 68 arrest warrants.
WHO IS ON THE COURT'S ARREST LIST?
Notable ICC suspects are Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, accused of being criminally responsible for acts including murder, persecution and using starvation as a weapon of war in the Gaza conflict, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, accused of the war crime of illegally deporting hundreds of children from Ukraine.
Israel and Russia, neither a member of the court, have repeatedly denied committing atrocities in Gaza and Ukraine respectively and have argued that the ICC has no jurisdiction over them.
When it issued the warrant for Netanyahu, the ICC also issued a warrant for Hamas military commander Mohammed Deif, whose death was confirmed after the warrant was issued.
The court has also issued arrest warrants for two senior Afghan Taliban leaders, accusing them of persecuting women, an allegation that the Taliban reject.
Prosecutors have requested warrants for Myanmar's military leader Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity in the alleged persecution of the Rohingya, a mainly Muslim minority. The outcome of that request has not been made public.
WHAT TRIALS ARE PENDING?
Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is due to go on trial on November 30 to face charges of murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity related to his war on drugs, accusations he denies.
A Libyan accused of overseeing a notorious prison is also awaiting trial.
WHY DOES THE UNITED STATES OPPOSE THE COURT?
While a US delegation was present for the negotiations that produced the court's founding Rome Statute in 1998, it never became a member and always opposed ICC jurisdiction over US nationals. In 2002, Washington even adopted a bill nicknamed the Hague Invasion Act, which authorises the president to use "all means necessary" to ensure the release of any US citizen or US ally held by the ICC.
In the years that followed, the US supported some ICC investigations, notably into atrocities in Darfur and Uganda, but remained firmly opposed to the court looking into alleged crimes by US troops on the territory of ICC member states.
During the first Trump administration, in 2020, Washington imposed sanctions on the court's then-chief prosecutor and another official over an investigation into whether American forces had committed war crimes in Afghanistan. That ban was lifted by the Biden administration a year later.
In early 2025, after the ICC announced arrest warrants for US ally Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, Trump authorised economic and travel sanctions against ICC officials targeting the US and its allies who are not members of the court. Washington has since imposed sanctions on 13 ICC officials including nine judges.
At the UN General Assembly last month, Trump called the ICC a "rogue institution" and "an evil group of people" and urged its members to resign.
WHY DOES THE ICC CLAIM JURISDICTION OVER SOME NATIONALS OF NON-MEMBER STATES?
Although the court is supported by many United Nations members and the European Union, other countries such as the United States, China and Russia are not members, arguing the ICC could be used for politically motivated prosecutions.
Israel is not a member and does not recognise its jurisdiction, but the Palestinian territories were admitted as an ICC member state in 2015. This, together with a ruling by judges, means the court can look at potential war crimes carried out by Hamas fighters in Israel and by Israelis in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.
The reasoning for the warrants for Israeli officials is the same as for warrants against Russian officials for crimes allegedly committed in Ukraine: they concern alleged criminal acts that took place on the territory of an ICC member state.
Myanmar is not a member of the ICC but, in 2018 and 2019, judges ruled that the court had jurisdiction over alleged cross-border crimes that partially took place in neighbouring ICC member Bangladesh, such as deportation and persecution, and said prosecutors could open a formal investigation.
The Philippines is not currently a member but was between 2011 and 2019, when the unilateral withdrawal by Duterte became final. Under the Rome Statute, if a state withdraws, the ICC retains jurisdiction there for crimes committed during the membership period.
HOW MANY PEOPLE HAS THE COURT CONVICTED?
ICC judges have issued 15 convictions and four acquittals. Twenty-three people have been held in the ICC detention centre in The Hague and appeared before the court, and 34 wanted suspects remain at large. Warrants have been withdrawn for nine suspects who died.
Of the 15 convictions, 10 have been for the court's core offences of war crimes and crimes against humanity. The others were for crimes such as witness tampering. Those 10 defendants were all African militia leaders from Democratic Republic of Congo, Mali, Sudan, Central African Republic and Uganda. Terms ranged from nine to 30 years in prison. The maximum possible sentence is life imprisonment.

articles.title: Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’?  Al JazeeraYemen conflict escalates as Saudi Arabia faces security dilemma  CGTNMore than 200,000 people displaced since fighting in Yemen began, says UN agency  ReutersNew IOM Data: Yemen Displacement Reaches 184,000  International Organization for MigrationBriefing by the UN Special Envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, to the Security Council (09 October 2026)  ReliefWeb
articles.full_text:
Fighting continues to intensify in Yemen as the internationally recognised government forces push a military offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, which controls part of the country.
Speaking at the United Nations Security Council on Friday, the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, said the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”.
Government forces are particularly looking to retake the important Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital trading chokepoint that has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have all but halted shipping.
At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in September, the UN’s migration agency (IOM), said.
Fierce battles across several fronts have prompted concerns from rights groups that Yemen has essentially returned to civil war after the relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014.
Amid the US-Iran war, Yemen’s worst fighting in years threatens to destabilise the region further, experts say. Here’s what we know:
What’s the latest on the ground?
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea. Riyadh has increasingly relied on it for oil exports amid the US-Iran war, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sunday, the Yemeni government announced the start of the operation “Dawn of Yemen”, which aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa.
On Saturday, it said it had conducted more than 2,750 precision strikes during military operations over the previous 24 hours, resulting in the “neutralisation” of more than 1,400 Houthi fighters.
The spokesperson for the armed forces, Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, said in a statement carried by Saba news agency that the operations also targeted high-value military assets deep within Houthi-held territory.
He added that ground forces “successfully” breached Houthi defences, recaptured operationally significant positions, secured their field gains and continued to advance the offensive according to operational plans.
The Bab al-Mandeb strait emerged as yet another front in the US-Israel war on Iran when the Houthis declared a blockade on ships linked to Saudi Arabia in July.
While the Houthis said that was in retaliation for ongoing Saudi blockades on Yemen, analysts viewed the move as calculated to provide more leverage for Iran amid on-and-off negotiations with the US – a close ally of Riyadh.
Battles are now raging around the strategic southern cities of Mocha and Dubhab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb. The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides currently claim control of the shipping lanes.
The Houthis, who have developed sophisticated weapons systems, including ballistic missiles, have also targeted Saudi Arabia with missile and drone attacks. On Friday, Saudi Arabia’s aviation authorities said three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, had been killed and several others wounded in Houthi strikes on the international airport in Riyadh – the first such deaths in the kingdom since fighting resumed. Several airlines suspended flights.
The coalition forces also heavily bombarded Sanaa, on Friday, with several injuries reported, including a child. Both sides are also fighting to control Taiz.
What led to the original civil war?
Civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis took control of Sanaa and imposed their own government in the capital. The seizure came amid dissatisfaction with the ruling government and following a revolution three years earlier.
A coalition of armed forces and local armed groups backed by Saudi Arabia launched military operations and restored the internationally recognised government in Aden. Fighting resulted in the deaths of between 150,000 and 227,000 people, while millions were displaced.
While the Houthis controlled much of the north, the Yemeni government controlled the southern regions.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 saw a lull in fighting and allowed aid to reach the deprived population, which has faced famine since 2016.
In 2023, the Houthis, who form part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” alliance of proxy armed groups, began disrupting shipping in the Red Sea in response to Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip. In March this year, the Houthis fired missiles at Israel amid the war on Iran, officially entering the US-Israel war with Iran which began in February.
Tensions escalated when the group declared a naval blockade of Saudi ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July, shattering the relative calm in the country since 2022. It followed the announcement with a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back Yemeni coalition forces from the strategic port city.
In September, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, leader of the Yemeni government’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a military offensive to “restore state authority”.
Is this a return to war?
Analysts say the scale of fighting means Yemen has fallen back into civil war as both sides come under scrutiny for targeting civilians.
As the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, declared that the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”, civilians, including women and children, are the ones bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.
The envoy stressed the need for the UNSC to support urgent mediation once more, although analysts have pointed out that recent gains by Yemeni government forces could mean they are more determined to push through the ongoing offensive, rather than agree to a settlement.
But “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now”, Grundberg warned.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, said: “It is beginning to resemble the 2015 Saudi-led coalition war on Yemen, when Sanaa and various other provinces were attacked relentlessly around the clock.”
A number of sites in Sanaa have been targeted, he said, including Sanaa International Airport. Several industrial facilities, including a chips factory in the north and a sponge factory in the south, have also been hit.
At least four telecommunications infrastructure sites have been struck in the capital and throughout areas controlled by the Houthi movement. Mount Attan in Sanaa was also hit by 10 air raids.
Mawry reported that, according to Saudi coalition officials, strikes have destroyed 136 military targets in areas under Houthi control, including military sites, launch pads and radars belonging to the Houthi group.
“Meanwhile, the Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of targeting public infrastructure and telecommunications facilities, warning that the campaign risks plunging the country back into a humanitarian crisis similar to the one experienced from 2015 to 2022,” Mawry said.
Will the United States take action in Yemen?
The US, which has previously indicated that it does not want to get involved in the Yemen conflict, nevertheless on Friday called on the Houthis to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, while demanding that Iran end its support for the group.
Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Yemen, Jeff Bartos, the US ambassador to the UN for Management and Reform, said Washington was “gravely concerned” by the Houthis’ recent escalation, including attacks on civilian infrastructure and airports.
“The pattern remains unmistakable. The Houthis act as instruments of Tehran to threaten freedom of navigation, undermine regional stability, and terrorise innocent civilians,” Bartos said.
“We demand that the Houthis cease their attacks against the legitimate governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia and we demand that Iran cease all support to the Houthis,” he added.

articles.title: US imposes full sanctions on ICC over arrest warrants and jurisdiction disputes - Jurist.org
articles.summary: US imposes full sanctions on ICC over arrest warrants and jurisdiction disputes  Jurist.org
articles.full_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio placed full sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday in response to continuing investigations into potential war crimes committed by the US and Israel.
“Our message is clear: the United States and its people are not subject to the jurisdiction of the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”
The sanctions permit the federal government to seize ICC assets in the US or controlled by “US persons.” There are some specially licensed exceptions, including 180-day grace period licenses giving the ICC and its state parties to address US concerns.
The ICC issued a response statement in which it condemned the action and accused the US of undermining international justice. The court wrote:
This measure targets an independent judicial institution, created by treaty and entrusted by 125 States Parties with investigating and prosecuting genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression. It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.
The announcement came on the same day that South African jurist Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize for her decades-long work in international justice. The former UN human rights chief, Pillay also served as an ICC judge and led a UN-sponsored commission that in September 2025 determined that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza during its military campaign in the territory following the October 7, 2023 attacks.
The sanctions follow from US President Donald Trump’s February 2025 executive order, “Imposing Sanctions on the International Criminal Court.” The order came in response to ICC warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant, as well as an ICC investigation into possible US war crimes in Afghanistan. Trump primarily relied on sections of the American Servicemembers’ Protection Act of 2002, which seeks to protect US military personnel from ICC prosecution when such personnel act to “protect the national interests of the United States.”
The US action represents an escalation in the ongoing adversarial campaign by the White House against international legal institutions—many of which the US helped create. In January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the growing divide between international institutions and national interests a “rupture in the world order.”

articles.title: Iran begins to crack under Trump’s silent war - The Telegraph
articles.summary: Iran begins to crack under Trump’s silent war  The TelegraphAmerica’s blockade is breaking Iran’s economy  The EconomistTehran measure to stabilise goods prices set for nationwide rollout, mayor says  Middle East EyeAs the blockade squeezes Iran, ordinary people pay the price of war  The Times‘The human cost of economically outcasting Iran’  Business Recorder
articles.full_text:
In the Caspian coastal city of Sari, Akbar, 43, breaks metal and hauls loads around a scrap yard for less than £4 a day.
His meagre salary is worth about half what it was a year ago.
Akbar recently started putting the little money he had left over each day to store food before another possible American bombing campaign.
But two weeks ago he started raiding those supplies in desperation.
“We can’t even afford our daily things,” he said. “And it’s not just me. It’s the same for most people I know, so I can’t even borrow from them, because they’re struggling too.”
Akbar’s quiet humiliation is the face of a slower and grinding kind of warfare now bearing down on Iran.
The bombing of major cities may have stopped, but another war has taken its place – one aimed directly at ordinary Iranians.
Washington has sanctioned all of the country’s airlines, throttled its border crossings and made it all but impossible to import medicine, food and fertiliser, as part of a US campaign called Operation Economic Outcast.
In September, the US Treasury blacklisted 27 Iranian carriers and aviation bodies, cutting off access to spare parts, maintenance and safety checks.
Tehran, in a complaint to the UN Security Council, described the measures as “economic terrorism” and “collective punishment” of civilians.
The success of the US blockade of Iran’s ports is also taking hold, with almost all Iranian exports now shut off.
The oil getting out belongs to Arab neighbours in the Persian Gulf – much to the chagrin of Iranian armed forces who have restarted attacks on tankers this week.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire' - BBC
articles.summary: Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'  BBCOil falls after Trump declares 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine  CNBCTrump claims Ukraine and Russia have agreed to energy ceasefire  CNNBacklash grows against Russia diesel deal as Trump claims Ukraine energy ceasefire  The HillRussia strikes power plant in Ukraine after Trump announces energy ceasefire  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.full_text:
Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent
Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.
The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post.
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it.
The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.
That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia".
"Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.
The BBC has asked the White House for further details.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.
Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
"All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.
For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.
Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.
Earlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday.
The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties.
Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports.
"Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".
Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.
On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal.
The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.
The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.
Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.
Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war.
Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said.
One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said.

articles.title: Former Harris advisor warns US-Israel ties may never recover from Gaza war - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Former Harris advisor warns US-Israel ties may never recover from Gaza war  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
Phil Gordon, who served in the Biden administration as then-vice president Kamala Harris's national security advisor, issued a stark warning in an exclusive interview with The Jerusalem Post on Sunday that Israeli-US ties have been severely damaged.
"It's really collapsed. There's no sugarcoating it. I think Israelis need to understand that," Gordon told the Post.
Gordon believes the damage inflicted on relations between Israel and the United States in recent years may be far more enduring than many Israelis realize, potentially extending well beyond the political careers of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump.
"I have rarely seen a turnaround in attitudes on an issue as rapid and comprehensive," Gordon said, referring to the dramatic decline in American support for Israel over the past year.
"You have a whole generation of Americans," he continued. "Look at the numbers on sympathy for Israelis versus Palestinians or favorable to Israel. It's really collapsed. There's no sugarcoating it. I think Israelis need to understand that."
Gordon does not rule out the possibility that the deterioration could prove permanent.
Asked why he recently described the damage to the relationship as "perhaps irreparably," he explained that his choice of words was deliberate.
"I write perhaps because I think it's still an open question, but I also don't rule it out," he said. "The more important word is irreparably because it's honestly possible."
Why Gordon is speaking out now
Gordon's interview comes a day after he publicly challenged efforts by Netanyahu supporters to portray a new book and interviews by Brett McGurk, a senior Biden administration official closely involved in negotiations over the Gaza war and the Israeli hostages, as vindication of the prime minister's wartime decisions.
In a post on X, Gordon argued that McGurk's account, while valuable, should not be treated as the definitive version of what happened behind the scenes.
"While Brett's front-row account is valuable, that doesn't mean it is definitive or its perspectives widely shared, including among former members of the Biden administration," Gordon wrote.
"I would say most of my former colleagues think that President Biden should have put more pressure on Israel to conduct the war differently and end it sooner," he added.
Gordon also wrote that few former administration officials believed Biden's biggest mistake had been publicly distancing himself from Israel, what he described as showing "daylight" between Washington and Jerusalem.
Speaking to the Post, Gordon explained why he decided to enter the debate over one of the most contentious periods in recent Israeli-American relations.
"Everything's charged and this is sensitive and important, which is why I thought it was important for me to weigh in with my perspective," he said.
His account focuses particularly on the efforts to secure a hostage agreement during the summer of 2024, including a crucial phone conversation between Biden and Netanyahu that, Gordon says, revealed just how difficult reaching a deal would become.
The July 4 call: 'We were not hearing a yes… but something closer to no'
On July 4, 2024, president Joe Biden called Netanyahu at what American officials believed could be a significant turning point in the negotiations to release Israeli hostages held in Gaza.
According to Gordon, Hamas had just indicated it was willing to abandon one of its central demands, creating what Washington saw as a genuine opportunity for progress.
To understand the significance of that moment, Gordon traced the negotiations back to the spring of 2024.
For months, Hamas had insisted that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released. Israel refused to make such a commitment.
That dispute remained the main obstacle throughout May.
But toward the end of that month, Gordon said Israel signaled it could accept a phased ceasefire arrangement in which a permanent ceasefire would remain the ultimate objective without requiring an immediate Israeli commitment.
"With clever drafting, we were able to put together the proposal that President Biden rolled out publicly on May 31," Gordon said.
Under that framework, Israel would not have to commit to a permanent ceasefire during the first phase, but good-faith negotiations over the final arrangements would allow for what Gordon described as "sustainable calm."
The proposal represented a breakthrough because it created a possible path toward a permanent ceasefire without requiring Israel to accept Hamas's original condition upfront.
For weeks, however, Hamas did not respond.
Then, around July 2, Gordon said Hamas finally agreed in principle to the framework.
"Hamas finally came around and sort of agreed, in principle, with the framework, including dropping its demand that a permanent ceasefire be agreed up front," he recalled.
"That felt to us like a significant step forward. Nobody was naive in thinking that this wouldn't be difficult."
With that development, Biden called Netanyahu on July 4 to urge him to move ahead.
"The plan was to really urge him to take the deal," Gordon said.
"This has gone on far too long. The hostages had suffered far too long. There was far too much catastrophic damage, Palestinian lives lost. Humanitarian conditions were horrific."
But Gordon said Netanyahu's response quickly dampened American expectations.
"I think we, the American side, were pretty deflated to hear Netanyahu say, 'Okay, you know, I hear you, Joe, but here are all the things that will have to happen for this to work,'" Gordon recalled.
Netanyahu then began listing those requirements during the call.
"I could tell in that moment that we were not hearing a yes or even a yes, I can work with this, but something closer to no."
According to Gordon, Netanyahu subsequently began what he described as "clarifying" Israel's position, clarifications that Washington regarded as effectively introducing additional conditions into the negotiations.
Philadelphi Corridor, Gallant, and the political question
One of the most consequential Israeli demands involved retaining military forces along the entire Philadelphi Corridor, the narrow strip of territory separating Gaza from Egypt.
Gordon emphasized that Israel had not even fully controlled the corridor when the original proposals were developed.
"In that sense, it really was a new condition," he said.
Netanyahu continued insisting on that position throughout the fall of 2024, despite objections from senior Israeli officials.
Gordon specifically cited then-defense minister Yoav Gallant, who, he said, considered continued control of the entire corridor militarily unnecessary and an obstacle to reaching a deal.
Another disputed condition involved an Israeli screening mechanism for Palestinians returning to northern Gaza, which would have required Israeli forces to remain in central Gaza.
In his earlier X post, Gordon argued that these conditions made an agreement impossible for another six months.
During that period, he wrote, nearly 9,000 additional Palestinians were killed, while more Israeli hostages died, including the six hostages executed by Hamas in August 2024.
He noted that both Israeli conditions were ultimately dropped from the agreement reached in January 2025.
Asked directly whether Netanyahu deliberately delayed the agreement to preserve his governing coalition, Gordon declined to judge the prime minister's motivations.
"I can't speak to or speculate about his motives," he said.
"I know there was a lot of talk that he feared that he would lose his coalition if he compromised on certain issues."
Gordon acknowledged that Netanyahu might genuinely have believed that continued Israeli control of the Philadelphi Corridor was militarily necessary.
"He certainly articulated over and over again that total victory was the only option," Gordon said.
But he added that the political implications were difficult to ignore.
"It also seemed to be the case that keeping his coalition together depended on rejecting that proposal, so yeah, you can draw your own conclusions."
Gordon stressed that no one could know with certainty whether greater flexibility by Netanyahu would have produced an agreement during the summer of 2024.
Nevertheless, he argued that Netanyahu's insistence on those conditions had a clear consequence.
"We do know that by digging in and taking the positions that he did, which seemed to align with his political interests, and certainly aligned with his emphasis on the need for total victory, that made any deal at that time impossible," he said.
A warning for Israel: Arms conditionality is now mainstream among Democrats
For Gordon, one of the most significant consequences of the Israel-Hamas War in the Gaza Strip is not merely the deterioration in relations between Netanyahu and the Biden administration, but a broader transformation in American political attitudes toward Israel.
Positions once considered marginal in debates over US military assistance have increasingly moved into the Democratic mainstream.
"Arms conditionality has now gone from a kind of fringe view to a mainstream Democratic position," Gordon said.
He pointed to the growing number of Democratic senators supporting measures that would condition American assistance to Israel, including legislation concerning Israel's planned development in the E1 area east of Jerusalem in the West Bank.
Gordon cited a Senate proposal he said virtually all Democrats supported and that would withhold assistance over E1.
Although the shift has been particularly pronounced among Democrats, Gordon emphasized that declining support for Israel is not confined to one political party.
"I know people are mostly focused on Democrats, and it's true there's sharper criticism of Israel among Democrats, but it exists in both parties," he said.

articles.title: Andy Burnham: Russia Interfered with Brexit Referendum, Warns of Ongoing Influences in Europe - SSBCrack
articles.summary: Andy Burnham: Russia Interfered with Brexit Referendum, Warns of Ongoing Influences in Europe  SSBCrack
articles.full_text:
In a recent podcast appearance, Prime Minister Andy Burnham asserted that Russia did interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum, signaling concerns over similar interference in the political landscapes of France and Germany. Burnham expressed that upon assuming office, he inquired about potential Russian interference in the referendum and received a definitive affirmation of its occurrence. He stated, “I’ve had the clear answer that, yes, there was,” emphasizing the need for greater public awareness about foreign attempts to disrupt democratic processes.
Burnham did not delve into specific details regarding the nature or scale of Russia’s activities during the Brexit vote. His remarks were met with criticism from Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, which argued that Burnham’s statements aimed to undermine the legitimacy of the referendum’s outcome, stating, “There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum.” The group expressed that such suggestions insult voters’ intelligence, implying they were easily manipulated.
During his podcast discussion, set for release soon, Burnham mentioned recent conversations with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, highlighting the presence of misinformation originating from Russia in German politics. He reiterated the importance of recognizing these threats to inform voters in both Germany and France about the political dynamics potentially influenced by hostile foreign actors.
This marks a significant acknowledgment from a UK prime minister regarding Russian efforts to sway the Brexit vote, despite prior warnings about the Kremlin’s attempts to exert influence over UK political matters. A 2020 report by Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee explored Russian interventions in UK electoral processes but did not conclusively determine the impact on the EU referendum results. The report criticized successive governments for inadequately assessing or addressing this threat. In response, Russia’s foreign minister dismissed the report as “Russophobia,” and a Kremlin spokesperson denied any allegations of meddling in foreign elections, despite the UK’s then-Conservative government expressing certainty about Russian interference in the 2019 general election.
Recent reports from BBC Verify have brought attention to the deployment of Russian-linked disinformation campaigns, including the use of artificial intelligence to create videos impersonating journalists and media outlets related to the ongoing conflict in Ukraine. Earlier this year, Vijay Rangarajan, the head of the UK Electoral Commission, warned that Russian deepfake technology had been “used extensively in elections around the world,” underscoring the potential vulnerability of the UK to similar tactics.
During his address at the United Nations last month, Burnham condemned Russian agencies for spreading falsehoods and exploiting public fears, announcing the establishment of a new center aimed at combating disinformation. A spokesperson for Downing Street reiterated the UK’s commitment to safeguarding its citizens and institutions against foreign influences, highlighting plans to enhance national security through legislative measures, bolster institutional resilience, and strengthen intelligence and police operations to mitigate these threats.
