Whatever marginal and transient impact on the price of a gallon of diesel that President Trump’s oil deal with President Putin may eventually yield, it will be dwarfed by the latest escalation of fighting in the Middle East.
If, as seems likely, the attack by the Yemeni Houthi rebels on Riyadh airport leads to a widening of the various interlinked conflicts across the region, then the economic impact will be as wide and profound as the humanitarian tragedy that has already brought so much suffering, especially, once again, to the Palestinian people.
The Middle East is no stranger to terrorism and war; but now for the first time there is a clear danger of a conflagration drawing in players from Turkey to armed factions in Somalia as well as from Israel to Iran’s border with Pakistan. Ancient religious and racial divides are creating new alliances all armed with the new drone and missile technologies, and, in some cases, nuclear weaponry, either existing or within rapid development. What such an outbreak of a more generalised war would do to the price of a barrel of oil can only be imagined and feared. The economic consequences would be felt across the world. In brief, there would be an energy-driven upsurge in inflation, interest rates, sovereign debt crises (including the US), and recession.
This is why the Houthis’ successful strike on Riyadh airport is so significant at this point. It is because the long proxy war being fought by Iran and Saudi Arabia for decades on Yemeni territory was almost a private affair, mostly overlooked by the rest of the world. The Saudis and most other Gulf states backed the Yemeni government or some other group while the Iranians supported and armed the Houthi rebels, also known as Ansarullah (“helpers of Allah”). The Houthis are named after their late founder, and the fight for control of Yemen, and with it the entrance to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, is but one contemporary emanation of the historic Shia-Sunni schism.
It bears repeating – because the White House cynically likes to pretend otherwise – that the current energy crisis and, in particular, the acute global shortage of diesel fuel is not primarily due to the targeting of Russian refineries by Ukrainian forces. It is, clearly, overwhelmingly caused by the Iran war, in which Mr Trump decided to join with Israel in February. That ill-considered decision then linked US allies in the region, such as Saudi Arabia, to the continuing conflict between Israel and Iran, plus Iran-sponsored groups in the “axis of resistance” – Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis. Yet, as has been seen in a series of attacks on lightly defended bases, oil, shipping and infrastructure in and around Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Qatar and Kuwait, the United States is in no position to defend its partners in the region, nor, at times, even its own military installations there.
The US remains the world’s single superpower with a vast nuclear arsenal and the most advanced weaponry anywhere, but it is demonstrably poorly equipped to deter a bunch of Yemeni gangsters with cheap drones and Toyota pick-up trucks taking over a strategic slice of the Arabian peninsula. Neither, on its own, is Saudi Arabia. Hence Riyadh’s decision to form a tripartite military pact with Turkey and Pakistan. As in Europe, so in the Gulf – America cannot be relied upon to look after its friends. If Ankara and Islamabad decided to deploy in the region, that would obviously broaden the tensions and be an indirect challenge to Tehran – they share land borders. Meanwhile, the Houthis are deepening their links with al-Shabaab, militant Islamists in Somalia, also prone to murderously asserting themselves in East Africa.
Such are the complex and unpredictable geopolitical consequences of America’s latest fatal entanglement in the region – precisely the kind of quagmire Mr Trump promised Americans was never going to happen again with him in charge. If things get worse, it will make Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq look like tea parties. China, Europe, Russia and virtually every other power has an interest in the flow of oil and the economic damage caused by these inexorably widening wars. They have to be de-escalated. But how? And who will do this? Asked about America’s response to the attack on Riyadh airport, and whether the US would join Saudi retaliatory air strikes, Mr Trump commented: “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
Perhaps. But it is difficult to see how America opening up yet another front in Yemen, the Red Sea and Somalia would bring peace and stability. The Houthis never surrendered during their previous long and merciless experience of being carpet-bombed by the Saudis, and there’s even less reason for them to do so against the US, because they realise that Mr Trump’s war is deeply unpopular in America, and they can see how US forces are experiencing overstretch and have failed to subdue Iran itself. Even if America just abandoned the region, the wars would continue, the fires now feeding themselves. Yet if Washington declines to act, then the Saudi government will have little choice other than to ask Pakistan and Turkey for assistance (and even ask the same of Israel, albeit covertly). Yet again America is losing control of events, and finding itself trapped.
One thing is, unfortunately, very certain and that is that the world will probably enter 2027 with intensifying energy shortages and a widening war in the Middle East, which even a change in control of the US Congress on 3 November will be unable to stop, simply because it’s now too late. So much, by the way, for the US and its “representative” Donald J Trump being awarded the next Nobel Peace Prize.

Will Saudi Arabia and Iran Go to War? What It Means for Oil
A declared war between Riyadh and Tehran is a minority risk for the next year. The proxy war on Saudi oil is already here, and the oil market is pricing it.
A declared war between Saudi Arabia and Iran is unlikely in the next six to 12 months, at an estimated 15% to 25% per this analysis. The war on Saudi oil is already under way: on Saturday 10 October a missile killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300 at Riyadh's main airport, per Al Jazeera citing the Saudi civil aviation authority.
The oil market is pricing that proxy war rather than a state-to-state one. Brent settled at $104.72 on 9 October 2026, per CNBC, and the risk that matters for the price is further damage to Saudi export routes, not a declaration of war.
Where things stand
The wider war began on 28 February 2026 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, and Iran answered the same day against Gulf states that host US forces, including Saudi Arabia, per Al Jazeera. The fighting has not been continuous. On 8 October President Trump said the United States would not attack Iran before the 3 November midterm elections, and the US blockade of Iranian ports stays in force, per The Star citing Reuters.
Saudi Arabia has been hit from three directions this year:
- Iran directly. Drones in Iran's first retaliation wave were downed over the Ras Tanura refinery on 2 March, and the refinery shut, per Anadolu citing the Saudi Press Agency. On 9 April the energy ministry said attacks had halted operations at several facilities, including a pumping station on the East-West pipeline, per the Saudi Press Agency.
- From Iraq. Riyadh said Iran-aligned militias in Iraq launched the drones that hit the Abqaiq processing complex in late July, per Al Jazeera. In September drones launched from Maysan province in Iraq hit East-West pipeline pumping stations, and the line was shut on 11 September; no group has claimed that attack, per Al Jazeera.
- From Yemen. The Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on 20 July, per Al Jazeera, and seized Mocha and Perim on the Bab al-Mandeb strait in mid-September, per Al Jazeera. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport was struck three times in the week to 10 October. The Saudi-led coalition blames the Houthis for the deadliest strike, which has not been formally claimed.
Riyadh has answered the Houthis, not Iran. The coalition said on 5 October that 100 jets had joined its air strikes on the Houthis, its first acknowledged strikes in four years, per Al Jazeera. The crown prince asked President Trump twice in September for US strikes on the Houthis and was refused; US support was limited to intelligence and targeting, per CNN. After Saturday's strike, Trump said the United States "may" join, per CNN.
Channels to Tehran remain open but narrow. Prince Faisal bin Farhan spoke to Iran's foreign minister by phone on 6 September, per Ajel, but Riyadh declined the first meeting between the Gulf states and Iran since the war began, per CNN. China, which brokered the restoration of Saudi-Iran relations in Beijing on 10 March 2023, per Al Jazeera, asked Tehran in September to help rein in the Houthis after a Saudi request, per Reuters.
The sharpest public warning came early. On 19 March, after Iranian missiles were fired at Riyadh and the Eastern Province, Prince Faisal said that "the patience that is being exhibited is not unlimited", per Al Jazeera. Seven months on, Riyadh has still not struck Iran.
The chances of a full Saudi-Iran war
- Estimate: a full-scale, direct conventional war between Saudi Arabia and Iran over the next six to 12 months is put at 15% to 25%. Source: this analysis, a judgement rather than a measurement.
- The more likely path is more proxy conflict, chiefly with the Houthis, and limited direct strikes.
Four facts hold the line against a full war:
- Both governments have strong reasons to avoid it. Saudi Arabia's priority is Vision 2030, its economic diversification programme, and Iran is already in a costly war with the United States and Israel and prefers pressure through proxies.
- The rivalry has been managed, not fought state to state, for decades.
- Diplomatic channels and third-party mediation remain open, if strained, with China pressing Tehran on the Houthis.
- Each side's energy infrastructure is exposed to the other, which deters both.
Three developments would raise the probability, and each is the fact to watch:
- Further mass-casualty strikes on Saudi cities or critical energy sites, by the Houthis or by Iran.
- A major US escalation against Iran that pulls Saudi Arabia in, which Trump has ruled out before 3 November.
- The collapse of the remaining de-escalation efforts around Hormuz and Yemen.
What the oil market is already pricing
The supply shock is measurable, and most of it has already happened:
- Price. Brent settled between $100.20 and $104.72 from 1 October to 9 October 2026, per CNBC, down from an intraday peak of $109.97 on 11 September, the day the East-West pipeline was shut.
- Hormuz. Exports through the strait were 8.5 million barrels a day in the week to 7 October, about 40% below the pre-war level, per CNBC citing Kpler. The figure swings: crude flows had matched the pre-war level on 28 September.
- Saudi output. Saudi Arabia told OPEC that its August crude production fell to 6.24 million barrels a day, the lowest since 1990, per Al-Monitor. Exports recovered to about 6 million barrels a day in September, the highest since the war began, per CNBC citing Kpler.
- The bypass. The East-West pipeline, the main route around Hormuz to the Red Sea, was back to 5.8 million barrels a day on 6 October, per Al Jazeera, against capacity of 7 million.
- The Red Sea. Houthi attacks roughly halved Saudi crude loadings through Bab al-Mandeb, per Kpler. Cargoes for Europe can still go north through Suez, so the squeeze falls hardest on Asia-bound barrels. Aramco deferred or cancelled cargoes to at least three European refiners in September, per Argus.
- Inventories. Global observed oil inventories fell by 507 million barrels from February to the end of August, 95 million of it in August, per the IEA.
- The buffer. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve held 282.98 million barrels on 2 October, its lowest since 1982, per the EIA. IEA members agreed a 400 million barrel release on 11 March, with 172.2 million pledged by the United States, per the IEA.
- Spare capacity. Saudi Arabia held 1.71 million barrels a day of OPEC+'s 3.80 million of spare capacity before the war, but effective OPEC+ spare capacity is now 0.22 million, per the IEA. Saudi idle capacity is shut in behind constrained routes, not available to the market.
The exposure is structural. Fossil fuels still supply nearly 81% of global energy consumption, per Al Jazeera, and the disruption has already lengthened shipping routes, raised insurance costs and tightened product markets. The KXCO AI Sector Ontology records a second channel: Hormuz also carries about a third of the world's helium, which chip fabs cannot replace.
The war map
Exhibit 1 draws who has struck what in 2026, which Saudi asset or route each strike reached, and where it met the market. Attribution follows each source exactly.
Exhibit 1. The war map behind the oil price. Each numbered link is a sourced claim, listed under the graph.
Three paths for Brent
The scenarios below are this analysis's estimates, not forecasts from any market source:
- Continued proxy war and limited strikes, the most likely path: Brent holds a $95 to $115 range with periodic spikes, per this analysis's scenario estimate.
- Major new damage to Saudi export capacity, or a sustained closure of both Hormuz and the Red Sea route: Brent moves toward $120 to $140 or higher as inventories draw further, per this analysis's scenario estimate. For scale, Brent settled at $118.35 on 31 March 2026, per CNBC.
- De-escalation and a partial reopening of Hormuz: Brent eases toward the mid-$80s to low-$90s over time, per this analysis's scenario estimate. Depleted stocks limit the fall, and Aramco's chief executive said on 5 October that rebuilding inventories could take up to two years, per Al Jazeera.
Further Saudi production losses would amplify every path, because Saudi Arabia is the market's swing producer and its spare capacity is the buffer that is now missing. The Energy and Commodities Center and the Live Trading News trading page carry the live prices and calendar.
What to watch
- Whether the United States joins the Saudi-led strikes on the Houthis, which Trump left open on 10 October.
- Kpler's weekly Hormuz export figures, published on Fridays, against the 8.5 million barrels a day of the week to 7 October.
- East-West pipeline flows against the 5.8 million barrels a day reported on 6 October.
- The IEA and OPEC monthly oil market reports in mid-October, the first official readings of Saudi output for September.
- The EIA's next weekly SPR figure on Thursday 15 October.

articles.title: Saudi-Houthi conflict in a ‘no peace, no war’ stalemate - The Manila Times
articles.summary: Saudi-Houthi conflict in a ‘no peace, no war’ stalemate  The Manila Times
articles.full_text:
THE full-scale fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi rebels in Yemen has for the moment taken the focus away from the bigger war between the United States and Iran.
Last week, a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people and injured 309. It was the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the US-Iran war ignited in February, and its impact could reshape the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East.
For more than a decade, the Saudis and the Houthis have been locked in a conflict that is driven by domestic instability, sectarian and tribal differences, and regional rivalries.
The Houthis began as a movement backing a minority Shiite sect in northern Yemen. In 2014, the group joined anti-government forces in a coup and took over the capital city, Sana’a.
Saudi Arabia, the region’s leading Sunni potentate, was uncomfortable with having a Shiite-dominated state for a neighbor, especially one that is closely aligned with Iran.
In 2015, Riyadh spearheaded a coalition of Arab states to dislodge the Houthis from Sana’a and restore power to the pro-Saudi regime. Iran stood by the Houthis, supplying its proxy with weapons, including attack drones.
Fighting raged throughout Yemen until April 2022, when the United Nations mediated a two-month truce between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis. The truce was extended twice before expiring seven months later.
Since then, a “no war, no peace” stalemate has settled in Yemen, with Oman activating back-channel negotiations to keep the two sides talking.
The stalemate crumbled in 2023, when the rebels began targeting commercial shipping passing through the Red Sea, claiming the attacks were launched “in solidarity” with other Iranian proxies Hamas and Hezbollah, which have come under heavy attack from Israel.
The last vestiges of the truce dissolved after the US-Iran conflict escalated into a full-blown war, and the Houthis intensified missile and drone barrages against Saudi targets. Riyadh has countered by launching air strikes on Houthi military bases and arms depots around Sana’a.
It used to be that the US was quick to respond militarily to any attack on Saudi Arabia, considered to be its most trusted ally in the Middle East. Today, President Donald Trump doesn’t seem too eager to respond to personal appeals from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for US military intervention. The reluctance could stem from a promise the Houthi leadership made in 2025 that it would not attack US commercial and military vessels in the Red Sea.
Another reason may be that Trump doesn’t want the US to be still at war with Iran when the midterm elections are held on Nov. 3, a situation that could prove fatal for Republican candidates.
Then again, Riyadh might have realized it was time to phase down its long dependence on American military might to shield it from its enemies.
That shield failed to stop Iranian and Houthi missiles from raining down on the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia, in fact, still wields enough influence to persuade Gulf states to enter into collective negotiations with Iran.
Omar and Qatar maintain back-channel lines with Tehran, and Riyadh could tap those lines to expand the scope of negotiations.
In 2023, a China-brokered rapprochement pact managed to restore ties between Riyadh and Tehran. The agreement, while hailed as a breakthrough, didn’t last long, as Saudi Arabia found out that Iran continued to secretly provide the Houthis with weapons.
Interestingly, Iran itself has volunteered to bring Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to the negotiating table. Iran, however, insists that Saudi Arabia must first lift its air and naval blockades of Yemen. Saudi Arabia says it will do so only if the Houthis give up control of the Red Sea coast and stop attacking Saudi airports.
Political observers say an alternative security realignment might work. Riyadh has integrated Turkey and Pakistan into the Makkah Defense Pact, a collective regional strategy modeled after NATO’s Article 5.
Under the pact, an armed attack against any one of the three states would be regarded as an attack against all of them.
The agreement is a radical shift from Middle Eastern politics. Perhaps that is what the region needs now.

articles.title: Warnock Uses Faith to Boost Democrats and Weigh 2028 Run - SuaraGarut.ID

Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock is using campaign appearances in New Hampshire and Nevada to support Democratic candidates ahead of the 2026 midterm elections while advancing a political message centered on faith, public service, and national character. His October 6 visit to New Hampshire also renewed speculation about a possible 2028 presidential bid, although he has emphasized the immediate importance of this year's elections.
Warnock, a Baptist pastor and one of Georgia's Democratic senators, campaigned with U.S. Senate candidate Chris Pappas and supported other Democratic contenders. According to WMUR, Pappas's campaign and allied groups faced a spending disadvantage against Republicans supporting nominee John E. Sununu.
Warnock also campaigned in Nevada, where Democrats are preparing for another competitive election cycle and potential presidential candidates are beginning to establish relationships with voters. In interviews with CNN and The Washington Sun, he presented faith as a public resource that should not be surrendered to Republicans.
Explaining his approach to spirituality during his New Hampshire visit, Warnock rejected the idea that religious conviction conflicts with practical reasoning.
"I don’t have any kind of hocus-pocus, spooky spirituality. It’s a faith that’s grounded in real life. It requires analysis, deep thought," Warnock told CNN.
He described his beliefs as compatible with evidence-based decision-making and a sense of responsibility beyond personal ambition.
"It respects data and science and hard work, but beneath all of that is an abiding sense that I’m a part of something that’s bigger than me."
Warnock connected that outlook to his desire to use his abilities in service of others.
"My prayer is that I can be used to do the most good with the gifts that I have," he said.
He also described his personal expectations for a life in public service.
"And I hope that at the end of the day, at the end of my life, I want to leave it all on the field."
Warnock said Democrats must challenge established political habits rather than allow institutional resistance to determine their direction.
"The Democratic Party’s like most old institutions. It’s slow to change. I feel that institutional inertia and I refuse to be bound by it, so I’m going to keep pushing this because what we’re faced with is so much bigger than party," Warnock said.
He argued that conventional political practices have not necessarily created opportunities for candidates with backgrounds like his.
"Old-school politicians who’ve been at this for a while, they have a certain way that they’re accustomed to doing this. And that way doesn’t lead to a Raphael Warnock in the Senate."
Warnock, the 11th of 12 children born to two Pentecostal ministers in Savannah, has built a political identity that combines his pastoral work with his experience as a Black Democrat elected in a Republican-leaning state. He has also become a source of spiritual counsel for some congressional colleagues.
Joking about those requests, he told CNN, "They ask me to pray, and some need more prayer than others,"
During his first visit to New Hampshire, Warnock appeared at events supporting Pappas, including a campaign-office opening in Swanzey. New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Ray Buckley said the senator connected with attendees despite the differences between the state's electorate and his Georgia constituency.
Buckley said Warnock's reception stood out in a state that regularly attracts politicians considering presidential campaigns.
"that’s not always a given in New Hampshire."
Buckley also described the level of attention surrounding the Georgia senator.
"I think that there’s great interest in him," Buckley said, adding that fellow Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff was attracting substantial interest as well.
Warnock's campaign appearances included criticism of tariffs, the Trump administration, and Republican policies. He characterized tariffs as a major tax burden for New Hampshire residents and argued that the administration had contributed to a damaging political climate.
"Donald Trump has unleashed a kind of evil and wickedness into the ether," Warnock said.
He also invoked the history of the civil rights movement, recounting a story about President Lyndon B. Johnson, the Civil Rights Act, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s efforts to secure voting rights legislation. In Warnock's account, King responded to Johnson's claim that he lacked the power to pass a voting rights bill.
"If the president doesn’t have the power," Warnock recalled King saying.
Warnock continued the account with King's reported response.
"we’re going to have to go get him some."
As a senator and pastor at Atlanta's Ebenezer Baptist Church, where King once preached, Warnock frequently urges audiences to remain active in the pursuit of change.
"Keep marching!" he tells crowds.
Warnock has also described emotional distress among members of his congregation. CNN reported that he recently delivered sermons focused on trauma, reflecting what he sees as persistent hardship affecting people in Georgia and elsewhere.
He said the emotional weight remains visible even during otherwise positive moments.
"wherever I go, whether I’m in Georgia or New Hampshire, there’s always just beneath the surface, even in happier moments, this heaviness."
In Nevada, Warnock framed the upcoming midterms as more than a contest for political power. At a gathering of faith leaders, he connected the election to broader questions about the country's moral direction.
"This is not just a political happening, but a spiritual undertaking," Warnock told the audience, according to The Washington Sun.
Asked how his ministry might influence decisions about 2028, Warnock described the country as approaching a consequential moment.
"an inflection point."
He said the questions facing the country extend beyond a single election cycle.
"But this is so much larger than the cycle," he said.
Warnock elaborated that the national discussion should focus on the values shaping American society.
"the character of the country, and it’s a big and important conversation. And I look forward to participating in that conversation."
He said he wants to demonstrate how religious principles can inform public life without requiring government to impose religious beliefs.
"countervailing witness of what faith looks like in public"
Warnock argued that Democrats should engage more directly with religious voters rather than concede discussions about faith and morality to their political opponents.
"I think Democrats make a huge mistake when we cede all this ground, when we cede all the terrain around faith and values to Republicans," he said.
He questioned why Democrats would leave those subjects largely to Republicans when he believes Republican policies conflict with religious teachings.
"Why would we do that? Especially given the fact that on matters of morality, in my view, they’ve got so much of it wrong."
Warnock also connected the role of faith communities to social isolation and technological change. He argued that increasing digital connectivity has not eliminated people's need for meaningful relationships.
"We are drowning in a sea of loneliness and hyperconnectivity. That’s the irony of the moment," he told The Washington Sun.
He said religious and civic leaders could help communities address the social challenges accompanying artificial intelligence.
"That creates a real opportunity for faith leaders and principled leaders in the political space to bring people together to address huge problems that confront us to deal with both the perils and the promises of AI, because it’s not going anywhere," Warnock said.
At a Nevada rally supporting Democratic Rep. Steven Horsford's reelection campaign in the state's 4th Congressional District, Warnock used a childhood memory about his grandmother killing a snake to illustrate his criticism of Republicans. He argued that the animal's continued movement did not mean it remained alive.
Horsford responded to Warnock's preaching style during the speech.
"He preachin’," Horsford interjected.
Warnock then applied the story to what he described as desperate actions by Republicans, criticizing their immigration policies and efforts surrounding the SAVE Act. He also accused political opponents of trying to purchase influence over the election.
"As you witness them doing crazy, desperate things, as you witness them trying to pass the SAVE Act, as you witness the cruelty and brutality of ICE, as you witness what Donald Trump is trying to do, as you witness folks close rank and try to buy this election, it is because they know that that old order, that old racist, misogynistic, homophobic, xenophobic order, is on its way out," Warnock told the crowd.
He has repeatedly criticized Republican officials who invoke scripture while supporting policies that he considers inconsistent with Christian teachings. Warnock described his willingness to challenge those positions as a contribution to public debate.
"service to the country," he said.
One recent dispute involved Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's use of a passage from the prophet Isaiah while addressing military officers. The passage was, "Here I am Lord, send me"
Warnock also criticized House Speaker Mike Johnson for praying before supporting legislation that he said would harm vulnerable Americans. At the Nevada faith leaders gathering, he challenged the relationship between religious language and policy decisions affecting health care and food assistance.
"They pray before they kick 15 million people off of their health care. They pray before they kick children off SNAP. They pray before they double people’s health care premiums," Warnock said.

Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay has taken a swipe at Donald Trump after winning the Nobel Peace Prize 2026, joking that she would offer to share it with him.
The South African judge and legal expert was awarded the prize for being “instrumental in ensuring war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted”, according to Nobel committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes.
He said it came at a time when ”the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack”.
President Trump has long coveted the prize and made no secret of his aspiration to win it. He has previously heaped pressure on the committee to give him the prestigious accolade.
“I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts,” the president told reporters on Wednesday. “No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled eight wars.”
At the Nuremberg court where Pillay was attending an academic and legal conference, she addressed attendees and made a joke at Mr Trump’s expense, in footage shared by Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnes Callamard.
Walking into a room of applause, she said: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”
The White House reacted furiously to President Trump’s snub last year and accused the committee of placing “politics over peace” when the prize was awarded to Venezuela’s Maria Corina Machado, a democracy and peace activist who challenged Venezuela’s autocratic government.
She later symbolically handed her prize to Mr Trump as a “recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom”.
This year, the Nobel committee appeared to be aware of the pressure surrounding the announcement and said: “We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law, national and international, underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice.”
Mr Frydnes said: “This is a message that international law and its institutions are the cornerstone of a more peaceful world. So of course, we hope that this prize also will strengthen the institutions, the individuals, not only Navi Pillay, but particularly her.”
Ms Pillay’s work has included defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid. She also served as a judge and presided over watershed criminal cases for the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

articles.title: Inside Israel's plot to kill Hezbollah chief as Netanyahu warned Biden aide would 'jump out of his skin' - Fox News
articles.summary: Inside Israel's plot to kill Hezbollah chief as Netanyahu warned Biden aide would 'jump out of his skin'  Fox News
articles.full_text:
As Israel prepared to assassinate Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in September 2024, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his senior defense officials disagreed over whether to notify the Biden administration ahead of the operation, fearing Washington could try to stop the mission, according to Wall Street Journal editorial writer Elliot Kaufman and a second source familiar with the deliberations.
"140%, they won't approve of the mission," Netanyahu told senior Israeli defense officials, according to Kaufman, co-author of "In the War Room: The Inside Story of Israel's Fight Against Hamas and the Iranian Axis," who recounted the exchange in an interview with Fox News Digital.
Then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant and IDF Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi favored informing Washington, believing the Americans might support a strike against a Hezbollah leader linked to the deaths of U.S. service members, according to Kaufman. Netanyahu, however, warned that then-U.S. National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan would "jump out of his skin" if he learned of the plans.
The disagreement reflected a widening divide between Jerusalem and Washington over Israel's military campaign against Iran's regional proxies, as the Biden administration sought to prevent the fighting from escalating into a broader regional war.
Hezbollah: Netanyahu's warning about Washington
When Israeli jets struck Hezbollah's headquarters in Beirut on September 27, 2024, the Pentagon said it had received no advance warning. Gallant spoke with then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin while the operation was already underway.
The strike killed Nasrallah, who had led the Iranian-backed terrorist organization for more than three decades, marking a major turning point in Israel's campaign against Hezbollah, which opened a second front against Israel on October 8, 2023, a day after Hamas' deadly attack in southern Israel, and had since launched repeated rocket and missile attacks on northern Israeli communities.
Kaufman argued that Israel had spent nearly a year waiting for American diplomacy to end Hezbollah's attacks on its northern communities, without success.
"From Israel's point of view, it had been sitting and waiting for 10, 11 months while Hezbollah had been pounding the north of Israel with rockets and with anti-tank missiles, waiting for American diplomacy to succeed," he said. "It didn't work. Something had to change on the northern front."
Kaufman said the confrontation exposed a fundamental difference in how the two governments approached the war.
"The United States may not have been in Israel's war room, but it could never be denied a seat at the table when it asked," he said.
"What I was told from the Israeli prime minister's office is ‘America's goal is to de-escalate the war. Our goal is to win the war,' and we saw that clash at every point, especially during the Biden administration."
October 7: Netanyahu's reluctance and the question of accountability
The book, written by Kaufman and Jerusalem Post senior military analyst Yonah Jeremy Bob, also describes how Netanyahu initially resisted launching a full-scale ground invasion of Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, only to emerge later as one of the strongest advocates for continuing the war.
"Prime Minister Netanyahu had just seen the IDF, Israel's military, fail miserably on Oct. 7, and Israel's intelligence services fail miserably on October 7," Kaufman told Fox News Digital.
Senior American generals dispatched by President Biden also warned Israeli leaders that a ground invasion could end in military defeat, even in Gaza City, according to Kaufman.
Netanyahu eventually approved the ground operation on Oct. 27, 2023, after weeks of internal debate.
"Over time, he would gain confidence in the IDF, regain confidence in the military, in Israel's intelligence services, and end up outlasting, exhausting, or simply firing all of his war room rivals," Kaufman said.
Kaufman was more critical when asked about Netanyahu's accountability for Oct. 7.
"I have spoken to Prime Minister Netanyahu several times in person, even more on the phone. I had a three hour conversation with him extending well past midnight in Israel," Kaufman said. "I have not heard him take responsibility for what happened on October 7th."
Instead, Kaufman said, Netanyahu consistently points to the failure of senior military officials to alert him before the Hamas assault began. "What he says is, 6:29. They didn't wake me up until 6:29 in the morning on the day of October 7th," Kaufman recounted.
Those remarks came as a new controversy erupted in Israel over the official record of Netanyahu's actions on the morning of the attack.
In a lengthy interview broadcast Thursday by Israel's Channel 12, retired Maj. Gen. Avi Gil, who served as Netanyahu's military secretary at the time, said that the prime minister's chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, attempted to alter the official record of a telephone call between Gil and Netanyahu.
Gil said a stenographer told him she had been instructed to change the recorded time of their first secure telephone conversation from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m. Gil said he had raised concerns about irregular recordkeeping with the attorney general's office in real time. Braverman has acknowledged seeking to change the recorded time but denied wrongdoing.
Gil also challenged the completeness of Netanyahu's public account of the events preceding the massacre, saying there were significant gaps between what occurred and what had been presented to the Israeli public and in his written statements.
The Likud party dismissed the alleged attempt to falsify the record, saying "the matter had been investigated by police two years earlier and that police had recommended closing the case because it lacked substance." However, prosecutors have not announced a decision to close the case.
Gil also said that opportunities to secure hostage agreements earlier in the war had been lost because of political considerations.
Asked by Channel 12 whether some hostages who died in captivity could have been brought home alive, Gil replied, "We could have."
He indicated that opposition to ceasefires and hostage deals from far-right ministers in Netanyahu's coalition influenced the prime minister's decisions.
While acknowledging that senior Israeli military officials believed Netanyahu was prolonging the war for political reasons, Kaufman challenged the argument that political survival was his sole motivation, pointing to Israel's subsequent campaigns against Hezbollah and Iran. "There were real strategic interests to be pursued," he said.
"Almost all of the real achievements of this war came later in the war," he said, arguing that the subsequent weakening of Hezbollah, the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria and the attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities complicated claims that continued fighting served only Netanyahu's political interests.
Iran: How Israel helped convince Trump to strike
The book also examines how Israel's early military successes against Iran helped persuade President Donald Trump to authorize U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities during the 12-day war in June 2025.
Kaufman described how a Trump administration official showed him a map of Israeli airstrikes that had opened a route toward Fordow, Iran's heavily fortified underground nuclear facility.
According to Kaufman, Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir subsequently made the case directly to Vice President JD Vance that American forces had an extraordinary opportunity to strike.
"You have a straight shot to Iran's nuclear sites. You will never have a better opportunity than this," Kaufman said, recounting Zamir's message to Vance.
Kaufman said the Israeli military chief told Vance that Israeli aircraft were already operating over the area, but that the U.S. possessed the heavy bunker-busting bombs necessary for the Fordow mission.
He credited the vice president with helping secure Trump's final authorization for Operation Midnight Hammer.
"Vice President Vance played a critical role in ultimately securing American participation in the highly successful 12-day war," Kaufman said.
The account challenges the notion that Trump was reluctantly drawn into the conflict by Netanyahu, Kaufman argued, portraying the president instead as responding to an opportunity created by Israel's demonstrated military capabilities.
Jake Sullivan's response was not received by the deadline.

articles.summary: Qatar sent over $100 million to Gaza during war – report  World Israel News
articles.full_text:
The figures reveal the scale of Doha’s continued involvement in Gaza following the October 7 attacks.
By World Israel News Staff
Qatar provided more than $100 million in aid to the Gaza Strip following the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, including millions of liters of fuel, food supplies, temporary shelters and infrastructure projects, according to figures disclosed Sunday, Israel Hayom reported.
The extensive assistance continued throughout the war between Israel and Hamas, even as the Gulf state maintained close ties with the terrorist organization’s political leadership and served as a principal mediator in negotiations over the release of Israeli hostages.
The figures reveal the scale of Doha’s continued involvement in Gaza following the October 7 attacks, which killed approximately 1,200 people in Israel and resulted in the abduction of 251 hostages.
According to Qatari government data, the country supplied approximately 30 million liters of fuel to Gaza between October 7, 2023, and the end of March 2026. The fuel was intended to support electricity generation, medical facilities and other essential services.
Last month, Qatar announced another agreement with the United Nations to finance the delivery of approximately 1.3 million additional liters of fuel to the territory.
The September 17 agreement was intended to support hospitals, medical centers and humanitarian operations, with Doha estimating that as many as 2.1 million Palestinians could benefit from the services the fuel would help sustain.
Beyond fuel deliveries, Qatari assistance included food, medical equipment, tents, temporary housing and projects designed to restore civilian infrastructure damaged during the fighting.
At a diplomatic meeting in New York on September 25, Qatari Minister of State Mohammed bin Abdulaziz Al-Khulaifi said his country had provided food, essential supplies and shelter assistance benefiting approximately 436,000 people.
Additional figures published by Qatar Charity, one of the country’s largest humanitarian organizations, show that it implemented 99 projects in Gaza between October 2023 and October 2025, with a combined value of 243 million Qatari riyals, approximately $67 million.
Those projects included 61 food assistance initiatives, eight healthcare projects and programs involving sanitation, education and emergency relief.
The revelations have renewed questions about Qatar’s complex relationship with Hamas and the extent to which humanitarian assistance can indirectly benefit a terrorist organization that exercises governmental control over the territory.
Before the October 7 massacre, Qatar provided hundreds of millions of dollars in aid to Gaza under arrangements approved by successive Israeli governments. The transfers were intended to support impoverished families, pay civilian salaries and prevent economic collapse.
However, Israeli officials and intelligence assessments have raised concerns that assistance entering the Hamas-controlled territory could strengthen the organization by freeing resources for military activities or generating revenue through taxation and diversion.
Qatar has repeatedly rejected allegations that its assistance was used to finance Hamas.
“Qatar has never provided money to Hamas,” the Qatari government’s International Media Office declared in a September 18 statement.
The statement emphasized that assistance was directed toward Palestinian civilians through arrangements coordinated with Israeli authorities and international organizations.
“Nothing was delivered directly by Qatar,” the government said, adding that deliveries were handled by United Nations organizations working in coordination with Israel.
The dispute underscores the contradictory roles Qatar has occupied throughout the conflict.
While hosting senior Hamas officials and providing the organization with a diplomatic platform, Qatar has simultaneously maintained close relations with Washington and acted as a key intermediary in negotiations between Israel and the terrorist group.
Its mediation helped facilitate hostage-release agreements and contributed to the US-brokered ceasefire reached in October 2025.
Yet the continued delivery of substantial assistance has also raised concerns about the possibility of Hamas rebuilding its political and military infrastructure.
Nearly a year after the ceasefire, Hamas remains a dominant force in parts of Gaza, while negotiations over its disarmament and the establishment of an alternative governing authority remain unresolved.

articles.title: UNDERSTANDING THE NEW AGE OF WAR - Dawn
articles.summary: UNDERSTANDING THE NEW AGE OF WAR  Dawn
articles.full_text:
“And what rough beast, its hour come round at last,
Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?”
	   *— William Butler Yeats, The Second Coming*
OPENING NOTEWilliam Butler Yeats’ chilling 1920 poem had a backdrop: World War I, the flu pandemic, the Russian Revolution and a sense of impending doom, an inflection point. The gyre is widening and turning again.
As wars rage in Eastern Europe, the Middle East and West Asia, it is important to understand what’s happening and why. Questions abound. The answers are not easy to come by, given the unknowns. Here I intend to analyse how we have got here and what lies ahead. In the final section I also discuss how we theorise about war and why.
Wars bring death and destruction. Technology helps. In our era, the pace of technological innovation (the Ukraine frontline is an example) has put Moore’s law on steroids. As the ongoing wars show, sequestering digital tech (like states did with nuclear weapons) and denying it to the adversaries is becoming increasingly difficult. Physical interconnectedness means the effects of war will spread beyond the spaces in which it is being fought; digital is non-spatial. Result: conflicts are creating ever more complex second- and third-order effects. War has become compounded.
Commanders no longer stand on a knoll and cast Napoleon’s coup d’œil, the glance to judge the raging battle, and dispatch runners with new instructions. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and its cascading effects is a case in point, as are strikes by Ukraine on Russia’s oil refineries that, in conjunction with the war against Iran, have created an oil refineries crisis, forcing US President Donald Trump to ask Kyiv to go easy on those targets.
Attacking Russia’s oil refineries is great targeting for Ukraine. Not so much for the rest of the world and energy markets. The war has also impacted US domestic politics and prices, not just the fuel price but also the bond market and its impact on mortgage payments.
From the wars in Eastern Europe, the Middle East and West Asia and the changing balance between the United States, China and Russia, contemporary conflicts are becoming longer, more interconnected and harder to resolve. Theories that once helped us understand war struggle to keep up. Attrition, technological disruption, economic warfare and geopolitical rivalry are producing conflicts with no obvious finish line and an international system increasingly incapable of containing them
Yet another problem is the finish line. X starts a war. Y fights back. Where in time and space does it end? Armies want decisive victories. Wars, increasingly, remain indecisive. Victory becomes contested. Iran against the US and Zionists; Ansar Allah against Saudi Arabia; Ukraine against Russia; the Taliban against Pakistan. This is not entirely new. Since World War II there have been many cases of tactical successes failing to achieve a war’s political objectives. That has now become a near-consistent menace for the stronger parties.
Allied with it is what I call the ‘arena problem’, a direct outcome of compounding. The clash percolates into ether (information war, influence operations, cyber-attacks), financial and commodities markets, shipping and insurance (resulting in energy volatility, food insecurity, shortages of raw materials in petrochemical industries, the list is long). The kinetic embracing the non-kinetic in a new dialectic.
The element of compounding and the absence of finish lines throw up another problem. War with its many battles is morphing into protracted conflicts that contain within them iterative wars and their battles, interspersed with pauses of uneasy, tenuous peace. As Nadia Schadlow, Trump’s former Deputy National Security Adviser for Strategy, has argued in a recent article for Foreign Affairs (‘America’s Attrition Trap’), belligerents increasingly have non-negotiable objectives. That leaves little room for compromise and makes conflicts intractable and wars within those conflicts attritional.
Gone are the days of short, decisive wars when “relatively small numbers of sophisticated and expensive weapons systems” could devastate the enemy. Conflicts are now long and grinding. The world has learnt that the US does not have the industrial base that can rapidly replace many of the sophisticated munitions it has expended attacking Iran. Worse, it doesn’t have a strategy to create the political conditions required for victory.
If attrition comes, can sustainment be far behind? No. Sustainment requires industrial assembly lines. The US won WWII because of its industrial output and innovation. It is now constrained by the inability to produce at scale. This isn’t a problem higher GDP can solve. As Schadlow notes, you can’t fire GDP from artillery tubes. That creates a gap “between nominal power and usable military capability.”
When a war is happening, military theorists study it even as events are unfolding. While studying an ongoing war is crucial, it is important to remain wary of applying its lessons to every case. This is not to say that every war is absolutely different in its conduct. Just that one has to be careful in selecting what could apply to one’s own context. The Zionist war against Hamas and Hezbollah is not the same as a war against Iran or Ansar Allah.
Sustainment and attrition are not new problems. The two great wars were all about attrition and sustainment. Attrition was taken for granted and it couldn’t be addressed without sustainment. Strategy incorporated both and industrial production responded to the challenge. That changed with the RMA (revolution in military affairs) in the 1980s. Lean became mean. Quality replaced mass in the field and scale on the factory floor. The wheel has turned again.
But before we proceed, a word is in order about the environment in which the present threats are emerging.
LIBERAL-INSTITUTIONALISM MAKES SHIP-WRECK
When the Soviet Union passed into history, liberal institutionalism declared victory. US political scientist Francis Fukuyama told us history had ended though, in fairness, he had borrowed the term from the German philosopher Georg Hegel, who had meant it in a teleological sense, ie history had achieved its ultimate purpose.
In his 2011 book, Canadian psychologist Steven Pinker came up with statistical abracadabra to tell us that violence had declined (Iraq and Afghanistan were happening). American political scientist Robert Keohane’s 1984 critique of hegemonic stability theory became the beacon for neoliberal policy. One-time US assistant secretary of defence Joseph Nye Jr gave us the soft power framework just before the demise of the Soviet Union. Power should attract and affect others to get the outcomes one wants. Culture and values played a crucial role, said Nye, as did foreign policy approaches that were grounded in legitimacy, cooperation and moral authority.
Nye has passed on and is beyond these concerns now. Keohane is witnessing the unravelling but has dug in (that’s a separate debate). But the point is that there was much rejoicing all round. It seemed the party was over for the Realists.
The Constructivists, a hybrid theoretical breed, were not to be left behind and found a backdoor to this victory ball. In any case, the long and the short of it was that, even without a world government, we were assured that we were close enough with the US as the benign unipole. Western and international institutions (the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, the European Union, the United Nations, the World Trade Organisation) were no longer just tools to manage the Cold War, they were the architecture of a new, rules-based, “liberal international order.”
In an ideal world, perhaps — the hegemon establishing a just order and submitting to it before demanding that everyone else should too. Rules applying in equal measure to everyone. Except, the world got liberal hegemony. The hegemon sets the rules but wants to sit atop them, while coercing everyone else into submitting. That’s when the bondsman decides, in a Frantz Fanonian way, to fight back. That moment births consciousness, the value that asserts that there is a part of human nature, a baseline of human dignity and right, that none must be allowed to cross.
Let’s now take a quick look at the current geopolitical scene before we round off with how we theorise about war. I eschew details because every item on the list can be written about at great length.
BRAVE NEW WORLD
John Mearsheimer marks 2017 as the end of the unipole anomaly. It’s not a random year but a structural pivot. Trump comes to power in the US and drops the language of the liberal international order. China’s economic miracle begins to translate into fast-paced acquisition of military capabilities. Putin’s two decades of efforts to resurrect and reassert Russia are succeeding and the US’ liberal hegemonic foreign policy now has rivals.
International institutions and norms, never much comfort for the Global South, are unravelling, as are the legal standards and norms of international law (witness Trump’s recent tirade against the International Criminal Court). While many states, such as Japan, continue to support international institutions, they have to walk on eggshells, because the state that provides them security is the one taking its own edifice down brick by brick.
The global state of affairs for arms control and non-proliferation is at its most dangerous and fragile point since the Cold War. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty between Russia and the US officially expired on February 5 this year without a successor agreement, which means there are no legally binding limits or mutual on-site inspections governing the strategic nuclear forces of the two. The 2026 Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference collapsed for a third time without achieving a consensus final document because of geopolitical gridlock. articles.title: Benjamin Netanyahu, Donald Trump criticize Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu, Donald Trump criticize Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
Awarding the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has drawn sharp criticism from both Israel and the US.
Pillay was given the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize “for her efforts to promote peace and international law,” according to the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
She previously served as a UN high commissioner for human rights and as a judge at the International Criminal Court, and later chaired a UN commission of inquiry concerning Israel and the Palestinian territories.
Nobel Committee's decision draws sharp criticism
The Norwegian Nobel Committee noted that this body, officially called the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including east Jerusalem, has drawn sharp criticism from Israel.
As part of this commission, Pillay’s report found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee said that she held states and national leaders accountable, brought hope to victims of violence and conflict, and demonstrated a firm moral compass throughout her long career.
“A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” the committee said.
Netanyahu responded to the decision by calling Pillay a “bigot” and the prize committee “misguided.”
“The Nobel Prize committee has lost its moral compass,” the Prime Minister’s Office wrote on X/Twitter. “It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the only Jewish state.”
Pillay’s “proudest achievement was to legitimize a corrupt prosecutor who turned to her fabrications against Israel, hoping that by joining her bigoted lynch mob, [ICC prosecutor Karim Khan] would beat a rape charge,” the post went on to say.
“Khan, who his own ICC employees accused of raping and sexually molesting them, used Pillay’s lies to build a fake case against Israel,” the Prime Minister’s Office continued.
“Now, the misguided members of the Nobel committee are honoring the woman who propagated this demonization of the Jews and this travesty of justice,” it said.
Israel accuses Pillay of promoting hatred and lies
The Foreign Ministry also condemned the decision, accusing Pillay of promoting lies, hatred, and blood libels against Israel.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a front-runner,” the ministry said, describing her report findings as part of a politically motivated campaign to demonize the Jewish state.
Further, the Foreign Ministry rejected Pillay’s genocide allegations, calling them “the biggest lie of the 21st century,” adding, “[Nazi propagandist] Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
Trump responds:'I've never heard of that person'
US President Donald Trump slammed the Norwegian Nobel Committee on Friday in remarks of his own, saying that the prize should have gone to the US, and effectively, to him.
“Despite ... [America’s] unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel Prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of. I’ve never heard of that person,” Trump said during a campaign rally in Syracuse, New York.
“I know a lot of people. I’ve never heard of this particular person, but congratulations anyway,” he added.Trump then said that the UN had played no role in the conflicts he helped resolve.
“In all of the wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations. They were of no help to me,” Trump said. “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t.”
Norway, where the Nobel Peace Prize committee is based, was also mentioned in the US president’s remarks on the subject.
“This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people who made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.
“The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really, enemies of civilization. And we will not forget Norway,” he said.
US imposes sanctions on ICC
Hours after the Nobel announcement, Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the ICC on Friday, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies. ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan condemned the sanctions, saying they would not halt the tribunal’s work.
The Trump administration has long been hostile toward the court founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. In the past, the Trump administration has imposed sanctions on ICC prosecutors and judges. Friday’s move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” US State Secretary Marco Rubio said in a statement, first published by Reuters.
“That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off its resources and crippling its ability to operate,” Rubio said.
The ICC deputy prosecutor told Reuters the sanctions “must be condemned.”
“The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing,” Khan said. “Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations, and our prosecutions.”
The sanctions are “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do,” the ICC said in a statement.
“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” it said.
“The designation is aimed at disrupting the court’s operations and at intimidating those who work for or cooperate with the court. The court, for its part, will not be deterred ... Yet the court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” the ICC continued.
Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Netanyahu, and a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.
Netanyahu also commended Trump and Rubio for taking the “critical decision” to impose the sanctions in a post on X on Friday.
“The ICC is not a court,” he said. “It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty. Thank you for your leadership.”

articles.full_text:

The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia, United Arab Emirates officials say.
UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi also alleged the pilot - widely named as Hamam al-Hammami - was last week trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport in a "suicide attack".
He wounded the captain in the cockpit with the emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was able to land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
Melbourne university RMIT earlier confirmed the pilot had studied there but left before completing his engineering qualification.
According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001.
"The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday.
"During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."
The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach".
"He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving.
This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment".
More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September.
In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia.
The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia".
Indian co-pilot Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero after managing to unlock the cockpit door while being violently attacked with an axe, allowing passengers to get in and take control of the aircraft.
Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by Flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.
Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.
He was later hired by UAE-based Flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.
Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.

articles.summary: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea  Al JazeeraNorth Korea fires missiles days after South Korea's hypersonic test  ReutersSouth Korea’s military says North Korea fired a projectile toward the sea  AP NewsNorth Korea fires unidentified projectile toward sea, Seoul says  USA TodayNorth Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles, the latest in a streak of weapons tests  NBC News

North Korea has fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, South Korea’s military says.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said one of the missiles flew more than 900km (559 miles) from the Pyongyang area on Monday. The joint chiefs did not specify how many missiles were detected.
Japan’s coastguard said on Monday that North Korea had fired two unidentified projectiles, believed to be ballistic missiles, which appeared to have already fallen.
South Korea’s presidential office said that Pyongyang’s repeated missile launches violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, urging an immediate stop.
Monday’s missile launch adds to heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula, as both countries have been conducting weapons tests.
Escalating tensions
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the latest missile launch appears to be a show of force since South Korea’s hypersonic missile test-fire.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.
On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
Last week, Seoul demanded an apology after a landmine blast wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone between South and North Korea. A joint South Korean-UN investigation concluded that two landmines were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago. Pyongyang dismissed the claim and accused South Korea of provocation.
Prior to the border mine blast, Seoul said it was conducting “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between Pyongyang and Washington.
Lee pledged to reopen dialogue with North Korea in his first speech after taking office in 2025.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons programme, while rejecting US and South Korean offers to resume stalled diplomacy.
Talks between Kim and US President Donald Trump abruptly ended in 2019. Kim Jong Un’s government continues to demand that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearisation as a condition for talks.

Kennedy was shot three times in the leg, but survived the attack and is now being treated at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Maryland.
Vectus Global was founded by Erik Prince, who also founded Blackwater, a controversial private military contractor which came to prominence during the Iraq War before being disbanded.
