A supertanker caught fire when it was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, officials said — just hours after the US struck a ship attempting to break its naval blockade on Iran.
The attacked supertanker, which was not immediately identified, was hit on its port side, causing a fire to break out, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations.
The IRGC shared video of the tanker ablaze in the water as it reiterated its threats on any ship attempting to cross the strait without its permission.
“A devastating fire is the fate of any tanker that violates the rules and disregards security in the Strait of Hormuz,” the military unit said in a statement.
At least 11 tankers have come under attack during the week that ended Oct. 4, the most strikes on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since the war began Feb. 28, according to the United Nations’ International Maritime Organization.
Another 10 strikes occurred last week, including one Monday that left 12 Indian sailors injured aboard the United Arab Emirates-owned On Peace oil tanker.
The latest attack came just hours after US Central Command confirmed that it took out a commercial cargo ship attempting to run the US’s naval blockade against Iran.
“A US military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew,” CENTCOM wrote in a statement.
The ship had allegedly docked at an Iranian port and was attempting to leave the region for international waters, CENTCOM added.
US forces have disabled four ships and turned around another 135 since it renewed its naval blockade three months ago.

articles.title: Mojtaba Khamenei defies ‘malicious’ attacks as US Army zeroes in on Iran’s 350,000 troops - Fox News
articles.summary: Mojtaba Khamenei defies ‘malicious’ attacks as US Army zeroes in on Iran’s 350,000 troops  Fox NewsLeader Lauds Police Force for Safeguarding Iran’s Security  تسنیمLaw Enforcement Forces Stood Firm and Resolute Amidst Wartime Conditions  خبرگزاری دفاع مقدسIran’s security indicators improve despite two wars, military chief says  ABNA EnglishMojtaba Khamenei Hails Police as a “Pillar” as Bombing and Recession Undercut Show of Strength  National Cou...
articles.full_text:
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei claimed Oct. 8 that U.S. and Israeli strikes had failed to undermine Iran's domestic security forces, praising police personnel for resisting attacks launched in February under Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion.
Khamenei's remarks on X also came as the U.S. Army released a new battlefield identification guide to help American troops recognize members of Iran's conventional military, known as the Artesh, whose ground forces were estimated by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security in June at 350,000 personnel.
"The criminal US-Zionist enemy's desperate efforts and malicious attacks on the pillars of social order and security, which are unparalleled throughout history, have not caused the courageous personnel of the Police Force to waver even a fraction in their mission," Khamenei wrote in a statement.
Khamenei specifically praised Iran's Law Enforcement Command, known as FARAJA, accusing the United States and Israel of targeting the institution responsible for maintaining domestic order.
"The focus and persistence of the criminal US-Zionist enemy in striking at the Police Force at its various levels, from its highest command levels down to those who are on the frontline, has only served to underscore the paramount importance of this institution more than ever," he wrote.
Iran's security apparatus comprises three principal branches: the Artesh, responsible primarily for conventional territorial defense; the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), tasked with protecting the Islamic Republic and projecting military power; and FARAJA, responsible for domestic law enforcement and internal security.
FARAJA, commanded by Brig. Gen. Ahmadreza Radan, is responsible for maintaining public order, enforcing the country's laws and responding to civil unrest.
According to Iran Human Rights Monitor, the force has evolved into a powerful internal security institution involved in suppressing anti-government demonstrations, monitoring political activity and enforcing the regime's ideological restrictions.
Radan has also been sanctioned by the United States for his role in human rights abuses.
The Treasury Department designated him in September 2010, citing his responsibility for beatings, killings and arbitrary arrests of protesters following Iran's disputed 2009 presidential election.
Khamenei also called for strengthening FARAJA on Oct. 8 through additional personnel, equipment and technology, including the use of artificial intelligence for data analysis.
His remarks come as the U.S. Army's Training and Transformation Command published a "Know the Threat" recognition guide Sept. 24, highlighted by Defense News on Oct. 9.
The guide shows an Iranian special forces soldier and identifies weapons American troops could encounter, including AKM rifles, Iranian-made Masaf-2 rifles, German-designed G3 rifles, MG3 machine guns and RPG-7 rocket-propelled grenade launchers.
The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the Ground Forces, Navy, Air Force and Air Defense Force.
A June assessment by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security estimated the Artesh's Ground Forces at approximately 350,000 personnel, including 220,000 conscripts.
The report found that the Artesh had suffered severe losses across its air, naval and air defense components during the opening phase of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign, while its ground forces remained structurally intact because there had been no ground invasion.
The Artesh is commanded by Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, a former Iranian defense minister who assumed command in June 2025.
Aside from Khamenei, Hatami issued his own warning Oct. 6, claiming Iran's adversaries faced "historic confusion" after failing to halt military production during the conflict.
Hatami also claimed that Iranian defense production continued despite American and Israeli attacks, saying the country's military production lines had continued operating during the conflict.
The extent of Iran's military recovery remains unclear. The Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security assessed in June that the country's conventional air, naval and air defense forces had suffered severe damage during the conflict.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said Oct. 8 that Washington would not resume military strikes against Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing "productive discussions" between the two countries.

articles.title: American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump - BBC
articles.summary: American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump  BBCMap Shows Trump’s Approval Rating in US Farming States After Diesel Tax Cut  NewsweekUS farmers are past the point of political return  TradingViewOpinion: The impact of Trump’s Iran war and tariffs on Johnston County farmers  The Wake WeeklyFarmers feel the squeeze in Trump country. Will they turn out for Republicans?  Star Tribune
articles.full_text:
Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.
In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.
Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.
With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.
On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.
Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.
The cattle market tanked immediately.
'It felt like a betrayal'
"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."
"It just felt like a betrayal," she said.
Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.
That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.
Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.
Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.
The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.
And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.
Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.
"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.
Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.
Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.
The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.
But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.
"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.
Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.
"It really makes a guy think," he said.
A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.
But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.
"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.
'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'
Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.
"The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said.
"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."
Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.
But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.
He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.
Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.
But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.
That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.
Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.
He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.
That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry.
"Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.
An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".
Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical".
But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt.
"We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."
But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".
Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".
"Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."
Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions.
"I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.
Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."
Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said.
Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.
But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.
"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.
He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers.
"I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"
Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state.
"They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."
All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on.
On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.
Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - don not pause for politics.
Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude.
"People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

articles.title: Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast as beachside communities and tourist areas prepare for impacts - CNN
articles.summary: Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast as beachside communities and tourist areas prepare for impacts  CNNHurricane Isaias makes landfall in US as another powerful storm barrels towards Mexico  Sky NewsA ferocious Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears  Global NewsHurricane Simon weakens to Category 3 as rains flood Mexico's Pacific coast  ReutersMexican president urges residents to shelter as Hurricane Simon approaches&n...
articles.full_text:
Category 4 Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter.
The international airport in Puerto Vallarta, a resort city on the shore of Bahía de Banderas, suspended operations as the powerful storm moved north-northwest offshore, along the coast of Mexico.
After initial models projected that Simon would make landfall on Sunday, the storm changed course and its path is getting harder to predict. It’s now expected to remain offshore through Monday, and the models are split on whether it will actually move inland or stay entirely offshore.
The hurricane is moving at a speed of 7 mph with maximum winds of 140 mph, according to the 1 p.m. ET report issued Sunday by the US National Hurricane Center (NHC).
The “extremely dangerous” storm is about 85 miles west-northwest of Manzanillo, a coastal city in the Mexican state of Colima, and 65 miles south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, in the state of Jalisco, according to the NHC report.
The national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency (CNPC), Laura Velázquez Alzúa, told reporters that despite the hurricane not yet making landfall, it is still “very close to the Mexican coast.”
But authorities are urging residents to take shelter, as the storm’s path is still somewhat uncertain.
“We ask that you remain vigilant,” Velázquez said.
The coordinator said that the effects of Simon — which include “strong winds, high waves, and storm surge,” particularly along the northern coast of Jalisco state — will continue through Monday.
The storm’s current projected path indicates that it has several “probable impacts” on certain states, which is why “Simon concerns us greatly,” Dr. Jorge Zavala, a climate scientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, told CNN.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, and Nayarit to remain in shelter “until an official announcement that the danger has passed” after the CNPC warned of “exceptional rainfall” and “intense winds” in those states.
“The wind and rain will suddenly and deceptively subside, creating an apparent calm that does not mean the danger has passed,” the agency warned in a statement.
Nonessential activities have been suspended, and precautionary evacuations are continuing, Sheinbaum said on Sunday.
Along the boardwalk in Puerto Vallarta, police reminded tourists that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter as the storm approaches, the Associated Press reported.
“We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” visitor Brenda Villareal told the AP. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”
Mexico’s Navy deployed more than 4,600 personnel to help with the response to the incoming storm, along with excavation equipment, heavy machinery, and other emergency resources.
As Simon moves closer to the coast, its heavy rain has already caused damage.
Federal authorities are working to restore power in some areas, including Acapulco, a coastal city in Mexico’s Guerrero state that was devastated three years ago by Hurricane Otis.
In Manzanillo, the Navy helped remove water from some houses that were flooded by the storm.
Manzanillo resident Cecilia Palomar told Reuters that the water started rising in her home at dawn.
“It had risen before, but not like this,” Palomar said. “Beds, refrigerators, heaters, all the furniture got wet, the whole house is flooded.”
The Pacific Airport Group (GAP) reported that the Puerto Vallarta airport will remain closed until 10 a.m. ET on Monday. Flights at the airport in Manzanillo were also suspended for the day.
Uriel Blanco contributed to this report.

articles.title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says - BBC
articles.summary: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says  BBCCaretaker killed and two teachers injured in knife attack at Poland school  BBCPolice detain dozens and check 50,000 schools after two attacks shake Poland  CNNPoland probes disinformation as officials warn of Russian exploitation  TVP WorldKnife attack at Polish school: in Ostroleka a student injures seven, two are in critical condition  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.
The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children.
"These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services.
Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.
A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.
It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.
"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday.
"In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.
The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right.
"Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.
A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".
Thousands of Polish police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.
Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.

Only Russia is responsible for the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday in a TV interview, responding to criticism from US President Donald Trump, who blamed him for high diesel prices and said he should be replaced.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday his country could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire, pushing back against US counterpart Donald Trump's call for Ukraine to pick a new leader.
"First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader", Zelenskyy told ABC News in a televised interview, a day after Trump said Ukraine needed a new president who would agree to end the war.
Zelenskyy said he told Trump's team that if they really wanted Ukraine to hold elections, "please tell Putin to give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections".
"We want peace, we are ready for a ceasefire, we are ready to begin with any kind of steps of de-escalation", Zelenskyy told ABC in a TV interview.
"And if the Russians want us not to attack their diesel, their refineries, etc., we are asking President Trump to give them a signal not to attack the energy infrastructure of Ukraine".
'Don't kill our children, we will stop attacking your diesel'
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data centre run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years after Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so", Zelenskyy said on X, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.
"Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel. And I think it's a fair deal", he added.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well", Sybiha wrote.
Trump vows for 'new leader' in Ukraine
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does", Trump said.
The US president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.

articles.title: The Nordics Are Rebuilding Their Transport Network for NATO - The Baltic Sentinel
articles.summary: The Nordics Are Rebuilding Their Transport Network for NATO  The Baltic Sentinel
articles.full_text:
Deeper ports, stronger bridges and expanded railways are improving NATO’s ability to reinforce its northern flank. Across Scandinavia and Finland, new military facilities and longstanding civilian construction projects are becoming parts of a shared defense network.
At Esbjerg on Denmark’s North Sea coast, dredgers have removed 3.7 million cubic meters of seabed material to admit larger ships. Near Narvik in northern Norway, a new military staging area covers more than 105,000 square meters. Across the Swedish border, railway yards and passing stations are being expanded. Farther east, Finland is planning to extend European standard-gauge tracks into its northern transport network.
Together, these projects illustrate a change in NATO’s northern geography. Reinforcement depends on the capacity to unload a ship, assemble a unit, carry heavy vehicles across bridges and move freight through rail junctions already serving civilian economies. Sweden’s and Finland’s accession has made those connections part of a shared defense problem.
The network extends across Denmark, Norway and Sweden — the Scandinavian countries — and Finland. Since 2022, it has gained completed facilities, new construction and additional investment commitments. But it is not a single NATO building program. Several major projects originated before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, driven by commercial freight, passenger transport or security-of-supply concerns.
Their military significance is now becoming more explicit. Governments and transport authorities increasingly assess infrastructure according to its ability to receive allied forces, move them across national borders and sustain operations farther east.
The Three Corridors
The strategic shift became explicit in June 2024, when Norway, Sweden and Finland agreed to establish a military transport corridor through their northern regions. Its purpose was to move personnel and equipment from Norwegian ports through Sweden into Finland, combining infrastructure investment with the removal of regulatory and legal obstacles.
Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre described a change from predominantly north–south thinking toward greater emphasis on west–east movement. Norway’s ability to receive reinforcements now mattered directly to its neighbors’ defense — and, the government noted, to the Baltic Sea and Baltic countries.
Norway’s railway directorate subsequently gave this broader idea a more concrete geography. Its 2026 freight strategy identifies three rail corridors, selected in consultation with the armed forces, as particularly important for military mobility.
Narvik–Tornio corridor supports the reception of allied forces and the onward movement of military supplies to northern Norway and its allies. The Ofoten Line forms the Norwegian section.
The Trondheim region–Sundsvall corridor constitutes another principal axis for Nordic preparedness. It includes the southern section of the Nordland Line and the Meråker Line between Hell and Storlien.
Oslofjord–Hallsberg route provides a third route for receiving and moving allied forces and supplies, drawing on the Oslo railway hub and the Østfold, Vestfold and Kongsvinger lines.
These corridors explain why investments far from the Russian border can matter to frontline defense. They connect maritime reception areas with inland routes and distribution points. A military corridor is therefore more than a line on a map: it requires ports, railway capacity, roads, terminals, staging areas and working arrangements between military and civilian operators.
Denmark Enlarges an Atlantic Gateway
Esbjerg provides one of the clearest examples of completed construction serving both commercial and military demand.
Its 21.6-kilometer approach channel has been deepened from 9.3 to 12.8 meters. Completed in 2025, the work enables the port to receive larger roll-on/roll-off and military vessels. The project received DKK 211 million (approximately €28.2 million) from the EU’s Connecting Europe Facility.
The same infrastructure supports increasingly large offshore wind shipments. Heavy civilian cargo and military equipment can require similar improvements in water depth, load-bearing surfaces and handling capacity.
In June 2024, the European Investment Bank announced a €115 million loan for the port expansion, explicitly linking the investment to European defense and vessels supporting NATO operations. The loan finances the broader development; it is neither an additional grant nor expenditure exclusively on military infrastructure.
Esbjerg’s military role predates completion of the dredging. In April 2023, Denmark’s armed forces prepared to receive approximately 30 U.S. Army helicopters and more than 1,000 items of military equipment and vehicles aboard the civilian cargo vessel ARC Endurance. The ship had also called at Esbjerg in April 2022.
Denmark is also improving rail capacity on the connection between Sweden and continental Europe. At Kalvebod in Copenhagen, construction of two freight passing tracks began in spring 2026. The approximately one-kilometer work area forms part of a project with DKK 712.6 million (€95.3 million) allocated.
The project originates in Denmark’s 2021 infrastructure agreement and supports growing passenger and freight traffic, including traffic expected with the future Fehmarn Belt connection. Its military role has been formally recognized: the EU selected approximately €42.76 million in military mobility support for the works.
The operational logic is straightforward. A port’s unloading capacity has limited value if the transport system cannot move its cargo onward.
Norway Builds Roads and Reception Areas
In northern Norway, a major road project is replacing infrastructure that constrains movement along the country’s principal north–south artery.
Construction of the E6 Megården–Sommerset section began in summer 2025. The 21.5-kilometer project will replace ten older, narrow tunnels with three new ones. Its cost framework is NOK 7.3 billion (€681 million), stated in 2024 Norwegian prices, with opening planned for 2031.
Norway’s road authority explicitly includes the project among improvements important for military mobility. Its 2026–2031 implementation plan also identifies upgrades on the E10 toward Sweden, work on the E14 east of Stjørdal and E6 improvements around Brandvoll, close to military training areas.
The authority connects better links to Sweden and Finland with allied reinforcement, Baltic Sea operations and potentially the resupply of the Baltic states.
Alongside these larger schemes, Norway’s 2025–2036 transport plan earmarks NOK 600 million (€56 million) for upgrading 14 county-road bridges important to military mobility. During the December 2025 parliamentary budget debate, the transport minister described the 2026 allocation as NOK 102 million (€9.5 million), up from NOK 50 million (€4.7 million) in 2025.
These are relatively small investments compared with a major tunnel project. Their significance lies in removing constraints that can determine what an entire route can carry. A road suitable for heavy military traffic over most of its length remains limited by any bridge that cannot bear the load.
One of the most tangible new military logistics installations is at Elvegårdsmoen in Bjerkvik, in Narvik municipality. On December 2, 2025, Norway’s defense estates agency, Forsvarsbygg, announced that the new staging area was ready to receive heavy allied equipment.
Covering more than 105,000 square meters, the facility brings together personnel and equipment arriving through the Ofoten region before onward movement into northern Norwegian training areas or east into Sweden and Finland. It replaces some of the improvised arrangements previously made around quays and sports halls.
Bjerkvik is national infrastructure developed to fulfill NATO commitments. Its purpose is to receive and assemble forces, rather than to serve as a new NATO command headquarters.
Ramsund represents a different form of expansion. The existing Norwegian naval base has a development program for 2025–2036 covering quays, maintenance facilities, access infrastructure and accommodation.
Forsvarsbygg’s 2026 update identifies some works as underway while describing other elements as early-stage projects. Quay maintenance and expansion at Seljevika/Ramneset had a scheduled start in spring 2026. That schedule should not be confused with confirmation that the wider quay development has been completed.
Ramsund is an expanding national naval support base, rather than a wholly new NATO logistics installation.
Railways Strengthen the Routes East
The railway from Narvik into Sweden is acquiring greater military importance without losing its original economic function.
Norway’s railway directorate reported in 2025 that work at Narvik station was underway, alongside plans for additional passing capacity on the Ofoten Line. It explicitly linked growing interest in the route to Swedish and Finnish NATO membership, while acknowledging that iron ore and commercial freight had long driven investment.
The proposed passing loop at Søsterbekk is intended to accommodate longer trains. Published plans targeted a 2026 construction start and approximately two years of work. Those documents establish the intended schedule, rather than confirming that construction has started or that additional capacity is already available.
Across the border, Sweden’s Malmbanan — the Iron Ore Line — is receiving substantial renewal and expansion. Trafikverket announced SEK 3 billion (€269 million) of work for 2026, including track replacement, yard reconstruction and overhead power upgrades.
